translation_en:
Preface to the Record of the Shuntian Prefecture Provincial Examination

We reverently reflect that His Majesty has inaugurated an era of dynastic resurgence. His sagely learning grows ever more luminous, and his illustrious virtue reaches the greatest heights. He has eradicated the abuses of the preceding reign and restored the established practices of his imperial ancestors, devoting particular attention to men of talent.

In the wuzi year of Jiajing [1528], when the Provincial Examination was due, your servant Li Shi, Prefect of Shuntian, requested the appointment of Examiners. His Majesty commanded your servants Han Bangqi and Fang Peng, Right Junior Supervisors of Instruction, to preside over the examination. The Associate Examiners were your servants Deng Shangyi, Acting Vice Director; Fang Yigui and Wu Lin, Secretaries; Yang Chunfang, Messenger; Xue Qiao, Instructor; Li Xian and Li Cuiran, School Instructors; and Zhang Shan and He Qi, Assistant Instructors.

text:
人耳其後乃一切皆用儒學之
官取人之途既狹而欲收得人
之効顧不難哉邇者
皇上用廷臣議畿内擇京官進士出
身文學著聲名者每經各一人

translation_en:
…the men themselves alone. Subsequently, however, educational officials came to be employed exclusively. With the avenues for selecting men thus narrowed, was it not difficult to achieve the desired result of obtaining worthy men? Recently, His Majesty adopted a proposal from his court officials: within the metropolitan region, capital officials who held the metropolitan graduate (jinshi) degree and enjoyed distinguished reputations for literary learning were to be selected, one for each Classic. The remaining educational officials were also selected more rigorously than before.

When the time came to enter the examination compound, the Investigating Censors, your servants Qiu Daolong and Wu Kai, who supervised the examination, made arrangements in advance, while your servant Li Shi bore responsibility as Proctor. There were 2,517 candidates who sat the examination, of whom 135 passed its three sessions—the prescribed quota. Upon completion of the proceedings, their names and the outstanding examples of their writing were compiled into a record for presentation to the throne. title: 嘉靖七年順天府鄉試錄
text:
皇上以非常之主龍飛特起而於文
衡之司今特用以非常之選者
此無他冀得夫非常之才耳責
望之深付托之重凡我諸執事
其不自懼以求自副乎此無他
其道惟公與明耳公則取之有
其本而不才者不得以亂真明
===
則照之有其道而不才者不能
以亂真明非臣等所敢知也是
維孜孜於公以求自盡而免折
覆之咎焉由是而求之非常之
才其庶可得乎夫
聖天子垂情如此諸執事戒慎如此
凡以爲諸士子也諸士子其亦

聖天子垂情如此諸執事戒慎如此
凡以爲諸士子也諸士子其亦
punctuated: 皇上以非常之主，龍飛特起，而於文衡之司，今特用以非常之選者，此無他，冀得夫非常之才耳。責望之深，付托之重，凡我諸執事，其不自懼以求自副乎？此無他，其道惟公與明耳。公則取之有其本，而不才者不得以亂真；明則照之有其道，而不才者不能以亂真。明，非臣等所敢知也，是維孜孜於公，以求自盡，而免折覆之咎焉。由是而求之，非常之才，其庶可得乎？夫聖天子垂情如此，諸執事戒慎如此，凡以爲諸士子也。諸士子其亦
translation_en: …His Majesty, an extraordinary sovereign, rose uniquely to the throne like a dragon taking flight. In appointing those charged with weighing literary merit, he has now made an extraordinary selection. This is for no other purpose than the hope of obtaining extraordinary talent. With expectations so exacting and responsibilities entrusted to us so weighty, should not all of us charged with these duties feel apprehension and strive to prove worthy of them? There is nothing else to it: the way lies solely in impartiality and discernment. Impartiality gives selection a sound foundation, so that the untalented are not permitted to pass for the truly talented; discernment provides a proper means of scrutiny, so that the untalented cannot pass for the truly talented. Discernment is something we, your servants, dare not claim to possess. We therefore strive assiduously for impartiality, seeking to exert ourselves fully and escape the blame of overturning the vessel entrusted to us. Seeking in this way, might we perhaps obtain extraordinary talent? The sage Son of Heaven shows such solicitude, and the officials charged with these duties exercise such vigilance and caution, all for the sake of the examination candidates. Should not the candidates also…

title: 嘉靖七年順天府鄉試錄
text:
知所自懼求以自副乎此無他
以非常之事業自期待耳今觀
諸士子之所陳郁郁乎慥慥乎
非道莫言也究義理皆斯道之
精微條事物皆斯道之殊散論
政治皆斯道之顯發即是而觀
之諸士子其能建非常之事業
===
以自奮者乎此無他行是言也
勿庸違焉耳惟時諸執事不負
其職而有以荅
聖天子之休諸士子不負其言而有
以慰諸執事之望矣此無他惟
我
聖天子非常之德覆冒如天地浸漬

以自奮者乎此無他行是言也
勿庸違焉耳惟時諸執事不負
其職而有以答
聖天子之休諸士子不負其言而有
以慰諸執事之望矣此無他惟
我
聖天子非常之德覆冒如天地浸漬
punctuated: 知所自懼，求以自副乎？此無他，以非常之事業自期待耳。今觀諸士子之所陳，郁郁乎！慥慥乎！非道莫言也。究義理，皆斯道之精微；條事物，皆斯道之殊散；論政治，皆斯道之顯發。即是而觀之，諸士子其能建非常之事業以自奮者乎？此無他，行是言也，勿庸違焉耳。惟時諸執事不負其職，而有以荅聖天子之休；諸士子不負其言，而有以慰諸執事之望矣。此無他，惟我聖天子非常之德，覆冒如天地，浸漬
translation_en: …know what they should fear in themselves and seek to live up to what is expected of them? This requires nothing else but that they aspire to extraordinary achievements. Now, looking at what the candidates have presented: how richly cultivated! How earnest and steadfast! They say nothing that does not accord with the Way. When they investigate moral principles, these are all the subtleties of this Way; when they set forth affairs and things in their various categories, these are all its diverse manifestations; when they discuss government, these are all its visible expression. Viewed in this light, might these candidates be capable of rousing themselves to accomplish extraordinary deeds? This requires nothing else but that they put these words into practice and never depart from them. Then the officials conducting the examination will not fail in their duties and will have something with which to repay the blessings of the sagely Son of Heaven; the candidates will not belie their words and will have something with which to fulfill those officials’ hopes. This is due to nothing else but the extraordinary virtue of our sagely Son of Heaven, which encompasses all like Heaven and Earth and permeates…

title: 嘉靖七年順天府鄉試錄
text:
如江河如臣等一草一木之微
孰不自盡其生生之化乎經曰
元首喜哉股肱起哉又曰帝光
天之下萬邦黎獻共惟帝臣其
惟今休歟諸執事諸士子其非
常之遭際何如也其非常之榮
幸何如也凡我諸執事其勗之
===
凡我諸士子其勗之
右春坊右庶子兼翰林院修撰
韓邦奇謹序

如江河如〔臣〕等一草一木之微
孰不自盡其生生之化乎經曰
元首喜哉股肱起哉又曰帝光
天之下萬邦黎獻共惟帝臣其
惟令休歟諸執事諸士子其非
常之遭際何如也其非常之榮
幸何如也凡我諸執事其朂之
===
凡我諸士子其朂之
右春坊右庶子兼翰林院修撰
韓〔邦奇〕謹序
punctuated:
如江河。如臣等一草一木之微，孰不自盡其生生之化乎？經曰：「元首喜哉，股肱起哉！」又曰：「帝光天之下，萬邦黎獻，共惟帝臣。」其惟今休歟！諸執事、諸士子，其非常之遭際何如也？其非常之榮幸何如也？凡我諸執事，其勗之！凡我諸士子，其勗之！
右春坊右庶子兼翰林院修撰韓邦奇謹序。
translation_en:
…like the Yangzi and Yellow Rivers. Insignificant as we, your servants, are—mere blades of grass and trees—who among us would not exert himself fully within this life-generating transformation? The Classic of Documents says: “When the head is joyful, the arms and legs rise to their tasks!” It also says: “The emperor illuminates all beneath Heaven; the many worthies of the myriad states are all the emperor’s servants.” Surely this describes the glory of the present age! You officials and examination candidates—how extraordinary are the circumstances you have encountered! How extraordinary your honor and good fortune! Let all of us officials strive! Let all our examination candidates strive!
Preface respectfully written by Han Bangqi, Right Vice Supervisor of Instruction in the Right Secretariat of the Heir Apparent and concurrently Senior Compiler in the Hanlin Academy.

translation_en:
Shuntian Prefecture Provincial Examination, Seventh Year of Jiajing (1528)

Proctor
Li Shi, Grand Master for Thorough Counsel and Prefect of Shuntian Prefecture. His courtesy name was Shizhao; he was from Anlu Subprefecture, Huguang, and became a metropolitan graduate (jinshi) in the xinwei year.

Examiners
Han Bangqi, Right Vice Supervisor of the Heir Apparent's Right Secretariat, concurrently Senior Compiler in the Hanlin Academy. His courtesy name was Rujie; he was from Chaoyi County, Shaanxi, and became a metropolitan graduate in the wuchen year.

Fang Peng, Right Vice Supervisor of the Heir Apparent's Right Secretariat, concurrently Senior Compiler in the Hanlin Academy. His courtesy name was Shiju; he was from Kunshan County, Zhili, and became a metropolitan graduate in the wuchen year.

Associate Examiners
Deng Shangyi, Gentleman for Receiving Virtue and Secretary acting as Vice Director in the Bureau of Evaluations, Ministry of Personnel. His courtesy name was Yizheng; he was from Yongxing County, Huguang, and became a metropolitan graduate in the jiaxu year.

Fang Yigui, Gentleman for Straightforward Service and Secretary in the Sichuan Bureau of the Ministry of Revenue. His courtesy name was Shifen; he was from Putian County, Fujian, and became a metropolitan graduate in the guiwei year.

第壹場

四書

在明明德，在親民，在止於至善。知止而后有定，定而后能靜，靜而后能安，安而后能慮，慮而后能得。

君子哉若人！尚德哉若人！

富貴不能淫，貧賤不能移，威武不能屈。

易

聖人養賢以及萬民。

揚于王庭，孚號有厲，告自邑，不利即戎，利有攸往。

歸竒於扐以象閏，五歲再閏，故再扐而後掛。乾之策二百一十有六，坤之策百四十有四，凡三百有六十，當期之日。

通其變，使民不倦；神而化之，使民宜之。

書

東流為濟，入于河，溢為滎，東出于陶丘北。

四海之内，咸仰朕德，時乃風。
translation_en:
First Session

Four Books

It consists in making bright virtue manifest, in loving the people, and in resting in the utmost good. Knowing where to rest, one becomes settled; being settled, one can become tranquil; being tranquil, one can be at ease; being at ease, one can deliberate; deliberating, one can attain the goal.

What a gentleman this man is! How this man esteems virtue!

Wealth and high rank cannot corrupt him; poverty and low station cannot shake him; threats and force cannot make him yield.

Book of Changes

The sage nourishes the worthy and thereby extends nourishment to all the people.

Proclaim it in the royal court. Cry out in sincerity: there is danger. Make the announcement from one's own city. It is not favorable to resort to arms; it is favorable to have somewhere to go.

Place the remaining stalks between the fingers to symbolize an intercalary month. In five years there are two intercalary months; therefore, twice place the remainder between the fingers before setting aside a stalk. The stalk count for Qian is two hundred and sixteen; that for Kun is one hundred and forty-four. Together they total three hundred and sixty, corresponding to the days of the year.

Carry through its changes so that the people do not grow weary; transform it with spiritual efficacy so that the people find it suited to them.

Book of Documents

Flowing east, it becomes the Ji River and enters the Yellow River; overflowing, it forms the Xing marsh, then emerges eastward to the north of Taoqiu.

Within the four seas, all look up to my virtue: this is the influence you exert.

第五道

問：宋儒有云：「求治之要，莫難於得天心，亦莫難於收人心。」又引蘇軾「躬信順以先天下」之言，而釋之曰：「無一事不當於天心，乃可言順；無一事不孚於人心，乃可言信。」至哉言矣！昔我太祖高皇帝謂博士許存仁曰：「天道微妙難知，人事感通易見。君能修德，則七政順度，雨暘應期，災害不生。」又嘗謂中書省臣曰：「得天下者，得民心也。恤其老，則天下之爲子弟者悅；恤其幼，則天下之爲父兄者悅。其心有不歸者寡矣。」大哉皇言乎！其得天心、孚人心之要道乎！恭惟皇上膺曆數於聖躬，建中和之皇極，百神具享，四靈畢至，此其時也。然星辰示變，加以風霾旱暵爲災，繼之螟螣，豈天心猶有所未得歟？際中興之昌期，圖更化之善治，四夷賓服，萬邦
translation_en:
Fifth Question

Question: A Confucian scholar of the Song said: “Among the essentials of seeking good government, nothing is harder than winning Heaven’s favor; nor is anything harder than winning the people’s hearts.” He also cited Su Shi’s words, “Personally embody trustworthiness and accord, thereby leading all under Heaven,” and explained them thus: “Only when not a single undertaking fails to accord with Heaven’s heart may one speak of accord; only when not a single undertaking fails to inspire confidence in the people’s hearts may one speak of trustworthiness.” How consummate these words are!

Formerly, our Emperor Taizu Gao said to Erudite Xu Cunren: “The Way of Heaven is subtle and difficult to understand; the responsive workings of human affairs are readily apparent. If the ruler can cultivate virtue, the seven luminaries will follow their proper courses, rain and sunshine will come at the appointed times, and calamities will not arise.” He also once told the officials of the Secretariat: “Those who gain all under Heaven do so by winning the people’s hearts. Care for their elderly, and all under Heaven who are sons and younger brothers will rejoice; care for their young, and all under Heaven who are fathers and elder brothers will rejoice. Few indeed will withhold their allegiance.” How great are these imperial words! Are they not the essential way to win Heaven’s favor and inspire confidence in the people’s hearts?

We reverently consider that Your Majesty has received in your sacred person the divinely ordained succession and established the sovereign standard of equilibrium and harmony. This should be the time when the hundred spirits all receive their offerings and the four auspicious creatures all appear. Yet the stars display anomalies; moreover, wind, dust haze, and drought bring disaster, followed by grain borers and locusts. Can it be that Heaven’s favor has still not been fully won? In this flourishing age of dynastic resurgence, as you seek good government through reform, this should be the time when the peoples of the four quarters submit and the myriad states…

協和，此其時也。然邊徼之卒反側未安，田野之民咨嗟不息，豈人心猶有所未收歟？書曰：「監於先王成憲，其永無愆。」今欲得天心、收人心者，舍我高皇帝，將奚法哉？然所謂修德、恤老、恤幼者，其道何如也？請敬陳之，以轉聞於上。

問：數載乎理，理寓於數；數非理莫立，理非數莫彰。理之備而數之顯，莫過於圖書。昔者畫出于河，伏羲因圖以畫卦，文周因畫以繫辭，筮者其用之一也。書出於洛，大禹因書以第疇，箕子因疇以衍義，筮者其目之一也。易至朱子作啓蒙，以盡乎蓍之變；範至蔡子作皇極，以通乎蓍之用。然易之揲以四，範之揲以三，竒偶殊，其用宜若相背矣。其分掛揲歸之法、通變極數之妙、考占成業之義，乃又參同契合者，何也？竊又疑之：易經四聖
translation_en:
…in harmony: this is indeed such a time. Yet the soldiers on the frontiers remain restless and unsettled, and the people in the countryside sigh and lament without cease. Could it be that the people’s hearts have still not been fully won? The Book of Documents says: “Look to the established statutes of the former kings, and you will forever be without fault.” If we now wish to win Heaven’s heart and secure the people’s hearts, whom should we take as our model other than our Emperor Gao? But what is the proper way to cultivate virtue, care for the elderly, and care for the young, as described above? Please respectfully set this forth, so that it may be transmitted to His Majesty.

Question: Numbers bear principle, and principle resides in numbers. Without principle, numbers cannot stand; without numbers, principle cannot be made manifest. Nothing surpasses the River Chart and the Luo Writing in the completeness of their principle and the clarity of their numbers. In antiquity, a drawing emerged from the Yellow River [?]. Fuxi used the chart to draw the hexagrams, and King Wen and the Duke of Zhou used those drawings to append their statements. Divination by milfoil stalks was one of its applications. The Writing emerged from the Luo River. Yu the Great used it to arrange the categories, and Jizi used those categories to elaborate their meaning. Divination by milfoil stalks was one of its headings. In the tradition of the Book of Changes, Master Zhu wrote the Introduction to the Study of the Changes to exhaust the transformations of milfoil divination; in the tradition of the Great Plan, Master Cai wrote the Supreme Ultimate to comprehend the uses of milfoil divination. Yet in the Changes the stalks are counted off in fours, whereas in the Great Plan they are counted off in threes. Odd and even differ, and their applications would thus seem to be opposed. Why, then, do they accord and tally with one another in their methods of dividing the stalks, setting one aside, counting off, and collecting the remainders; in their subtleties of comprehending transformations and exhausting numbers; and in their principles of examining prognostications and accomplishing undertakings? I venture to raise a further doubt: the Changes passed through the hands of four sages…

無七八之文也何自而占乎不知於孔

河圖洛書數之大者也諸士子究心久
矣其詳言之勿隱
===
問威天下在乎兵而主兵者在於將吳子
有言三軍之衆百萬之師張設輕重在
於一人將固不可以不知兵矣嘗即一
二兵法而觀之途有所不由也不由崤
澠者成七國之功由壺頭者致五溪之
敗城有所不攻也不攻華費者完兵而
深入攻郢郡者衆潰而走死君命有所
不受也叱吳使之說者成霸越之功拒
長史之謀者舍格天之業士卒當如愛
punctuated:
而始成。範乃成於蔡子一人之手，而其數之妙直與大易同流，似非三代以還儒者之所能到也。其或别有所授乎？易爻用變，今載之經惟九六耳。朱子筮儀，四爻五爻之變，乃用之卦不變之交。易無七八之爻也，何自而占乎？不知於孔子大傳之說合乎否乎？抑亦别有說乎？河圖洛書，數之大者也。諸士子究心久矣，其詳言之，勿隱。

問：威天下在乎兵，而主兵者在於將。吳子有言：「三軍之衆，百萬之師，張設輕重，在於一人。」將固不可以不知兵矣。嘗即一二兵法而觀之：途有所不由也，不由崤澠者成七國之功，由壺頭者致五溪之敗；城有所不攻也，不攻華費者完兵而深入，攻郢郡者衆潰而走死；君命有所不受也，叱吳使之說者成霸越之功，拒長史之謀者舍格天之業。士卒當如愛
translation_en:
…and only then was it completed. Yet the scheme of the Great Plan was completed by Master Cai alone, and the subtlety of its numbers ranks directly alongside that of the great Book of Changes. This seems beyond what scholars since the Three Dynasties could have achieved. Might he have received some other transmission?

The lines of the Changes employ change; what is recorded in the classic consists only of nines and sixes. Yet in Master Zhu’s Procedures for Divination, when four or five lines change, one uses the unchanging lines of the resulting hexagram [the transcription’s 交 apparently stands for 爻, “line”]. The Changes has no lines designated seven or eight: on what basis, then, does one divine? Does this accord with Confucius’s explanation in the Great Commentary, or not? Or is there some other explanation? The River Chart and Luo Writing are the foremost expressions of numerical principles. You candidates have long studied these matters closely. Explain them in detail, holding nothing back.

Question: Inspiring awe throughout the realm depends on military forces, and command of military forces rests with generals. Master Wu said: “Whether the assembled armies, a host of a million, carry weight when deployed depends on a single man.” A general certainly cannot afford to be ignorant of warfare. Consider one or two principles of military strategy. There are roads one should not take: avoiding Xiao and Mian brought success against the Seven Kingdoms, whereas taking the route through Hutou led to defeat among the Five Streams. There are cities one should not attack: refraining from attacking Hua and Fei preserved the army intact for a deep advance, whereas attacking Ying Commandery [?] brought the army’s collapse and the commander’s death in flight. There are commands from the ruler one should not accept: rebuffing the arguments of the envoy from Wu secured Yue’s hegemony, whereas rejecting the Chief Clerk’s plan meant abandoning an undertaking that could move Heaven [?]. Soldiers should be treated as one loves…

title: 嘉靖七年順天府鄉試錄
text:
子也與士卒分勞苦者著績于河西不
恤士卒饑寒者見殺於安陽數將於兵
法合之則成違之則敗是固然矣然有
可疑者爭北山而敗高陵不可向也或
以蹙馬鞍山而取勝以卒神而勝妖術
似可用也或以用六甲而致敗臨泜水
而退舍全軍宜矣何退舍澗水者卒至
喪師日夜行三百里敗走宜矣何日夜
行二百里者卒至成功是又於兵法也
===
或同合而成敗頓殊或同違而勝負特
異然則為將者將無事於兵法乎其或
兵法之變有非可以常法拘乎文事武
備皆諸士子分內事也毋曰吾儒生未
學於軍旅
問宋之盛時群賢滿朝併志協德共成治
化可謂美矣然亦有不盡同者請為諸
士誦之同議伐契丹也一則謂狂寇易
滅當速發兵以誅之一則謂儲廩未備

可疑者爭北山而敗高陵不可向也或
以處馬歎山而取勝以卒神而勝妖術
似可用也或以用六甲而致敗臨泜水
而退舍金軍宜矣何退舍㵎水者卒至
喪師日夜行三百里敗走宜矣何日夜
行二百里者卒至成功是又於兵法也
===

異然則爲將者將無事於兵法乎其或
兵法之變有非可以常法拘乎文事武
備皆諸士子分內事也毋曰吾儒生未
學於軍旅
問宋之盛時群賢滿朝併志協德共成治
化可謂美矣然亦有不盡同者請爲諸
士誦之同議伐契丹也一則謂狂寇易
滅當遠發兵以誅之一則謂儲廩未備
punctuated:
子也。與士卒分勞苦者，著績于河西；不恤士卒饑寒者，見殺於安陽。數將於兵法，合之則成，違之則敗，是固然矣。然有可疑者：爭北山而敗，高陵不可向也；或以蹙馬鞍山而取勝。以卒神而勝，妖術似可用也；或以用六甲而致敗。臨泜水而退舍，全軍宜矣；何退舍澗水者，卒至喪師？日夜行三百里，敗走宜矣；何日夜行二百里者，卒至成功？是又於兵法也，或同合而成敗頓殊，或同違而勝負特異。然則為將者，將無事於兵法乎？其或兵法之變，有非可以常法拘乎？文事武備，皆諸士子分內事也。毋曰吾儒生，未學於軍旅。
問：宋之盛時，群賢滿朝，併志協德，共成治化，可謂美矣。然亦有不盡同者，請為諸士誦之。同議伐契丹也，一則謂狂寇易滅，當速發兵以誅之；一則謂儲廩未備，
translation_en:
…as one's children. The commander who shared his soldiers’ hardships won distinction in Hexi; the one who showed no concern for their hunger and cold was killed at Anyang. These commanders succeeded when they conformed to the arts of war and failed when they departed from them: this is certainly so. Yet there are points that invite doubt. One commander fought for Beishan and was defeated—high ground should not be attacked; yet another won by pressing an attack on Ma’anshan. One won by employing “soldier spirits” [?], suggesting that sorcery might be useful; yet another suffered defeat through employing the spirits of the Six Jia. When a commander withdrew his encampment upon reaching the Zhi River, it was fitting that he preserved his army intact; why, then, did one who withdrew his encampment at the Jian River ultimately lose his army? When a commander marched three hundred li in a day and night, it was fitting that he was defeated and fled; why, then, did one who marched two hundred li in a day and night ultimately succeed? Here again, in relation to the arts of war, some equally conformed to them, yet their success and failure differed utterly; others equally departed from them, yet their victory and defeat were strikingly different. Does this mean that commanders have no need of the arts of war? Or might their adaptations include things that cannot be confined within fixed rules? Civil affairs and military preparedness alike fall within the responsibilities of you examination candidates. Do not say, “We are Confucian scholars and have not studied military affairs.”
Question: At the height of the Song dynasty, worthy men filled the court. United in purpose and harmonious in virtue, they together brought about good government and moral transformation. This may indeed be called admirable. Yet there were also matters on which they did not entirely agree. Allow me to recount them for you candidates. When discussing an attack on the Khitan, one said that the reckless invaders could easily be destroyed and that troops should be dispatched swiftly to punish them; another said that the granary reserves were not yet ready…

title: 嘉靖七年順天府鄉試錄
text:
當施方畧以制之所謂固自有體者然
歟同尹開封也一則威嚴御下名震都
邑一則簡易循理不求近名所謂各用
其所長者然歟三朝大臣則禮不得不
恭布衣召用則道不敢不重同事幼主
也而所見不同如此然則恭倨之說似
歟為世臣則歸朝以見上為諍臣則退
處以自守同論新法也而所處不同如
此然則優劣之論似歟易曰君子以同
===
===
而異語曰君子和而不同豈謂是歟請
試言之
問天下之大勢在外則邊陲在內則郡邑
邊陲所以禦外侮郡邑所以安內治也
今邊陲之上軍士怯怠矣紀綱陵遲矣
帑藏空虛矣其何以禦外乎郡邑之中
風俗頹敗矣盜賊竊發矣生民困瘁矣
安在其安內乎致是者厥咎何由也今
所以處之者何道也遐想古之人教歩

也而所見不同如此然則恭倨之說似
歟爲世臣則歸朝以見上爲諍臣則退
處以自守同論新法也而所處不同如
此然則優劣之論似歟易曰君子以同
而異語曰君子和而不同豈謂是歟請
試言之
===
問天下之大勢在外則邊陲在内則郡邑
邊陲所以禦外侮郡邑所以安内治也
今邊陲之上軍士怯息矣紀綱陵遲矣
帑藏空虚矣其何以禦外乎郡邑之中
風俗頽敗矣盜賊竊發矣生民困瘁矣
安在其安内乎致是者厥咎何由也今
所以處之者何道也遐想古之人教步
punctuated:
當施方畧以制之。所謂固自有體者，然歟？同尹開封也，一則威嚴御下，名震都邑；一則簡易循理，不求近名。所謂各用其所長者，然歟？三朝大臣，則禮不得不恭；布衣召用，則道不敢不重。同事幼主也，而所見不同如此，然則恭倨之說似歟？為世臣，則歸朝以見上；為諍臣，則退處以自守。同論新法也，而所處不同如此，然則優劣之論似歟？《易》曰：「君子以同而異。」《語》曰：「君子和而不同。」豈謂是歟？請試言之。
問：天下之大勢，在外則邊陲，在內則郡邑。邊陲所以禦外侮，郡邑所以安內治也。今邊陲之上，軍士怯怠矣，紀綱陵遲矣，帑藏空虛矣，其何以禦外乎？郡邑之中，風俗頹敗矣，盜賊竊發矣，生民困瘁矣，安在其安內乎？致是者，厥咎何由也？今所以處之者，何道也？遐想古之人教歩
translation_en:
…one should employ plans and strategies to bring them under control. Is this what is meant by saying that each certainly has his own proper approach? Both served as Prefect of Kaifeng: one governed his subordinates with stern authority, his reputation inspiring awe throughout the capital; the other proceeded with simplicity and ease, following sound principles without seeking immediate renown. Is this what is meant by each employing his particular strengths? For a senior minister who had served three reigns, ceremonial conduct necessarily had to be respectful; for a commoner summoned to office, the Way necessarily had to be held in high esteem. Both served a young sovereign, yet their views differed so greatly. Is it therefore fitting to characterize them as deferential and arrogant? As a hereditary servant of the dynasty, one returned to court to have an audience with the emperor; as a remonstrating minister, the other withdrew to preserve his integrity. Both expressed views on the New Policies, yet the courses they took differed so greatly. Is it therefore fitting to judge one superior and the other inferior? The Book of Changes says: “The gentleman finds common ground while retaining differences.” The Analects says: “The gentleman is harmonious without being conformist.” Do these statements refer to this? Please offer your explanation.
Question: The overall strategic situation of the realm rests externally upon the frontiers and internally upon the prefectures and counties. The frontiers serve to repel foreign aggression; the prefectures and counties serve to secure domestic order. Now, along the frontiers, soldiers are timid and indolent, discipline has deteriorated, and the treasuries are empty. How, then, can they repel external threats? Within the prefectures and counties, customs have decayed, bandits have sprung up, and the people are impoverished and exhausted. Where, then, is the security of domestic order? What is the source of the fault that has brought matters to this point? By what means should this now be addressed? Reflecting upon men of antiquity, there was one who trained infantry…

title: 嘉靖七年順天府鄉試錄
text:
兵于澤潞者天下推勇誅亂將于朔方
者諸鎮奉法屯要害浚溝渠而興屯田
者羌夷降敗是皆名將也得是人而用
之軍氣可振帑藏可足紀綱可伸歟守
蜀郡者治崇禮義長朝歌者人稱神明
勸農桑重牧養而禁奢侈者郡有蓄積
是皆良吏也得是人而用之民生可蘇
盜賊可息風俗可淳歟古人未嘗借才
于異代今天下文武之士歲進幾千人
===
獨無是人出于其間歟抑或有之而莫
之用歟此天下剥膚之弊而
廟堂之所欲聞者也諸士子其縱言之主司
者為之達

punctuated: 兵于澤潞者，天下推勇；誅亂將于朔方者，諸鎮奉法；屯要害、浚溝渠而興屯田者，羌夷降敗。是皆名將也。得是人而用之，軍氣可振、帑藏可足、紀綱可伸歟？守蜀郡者，治崇禮義；長朝歌者，人稱神明；勸農桑、重牧養而禁奢侈者，郡有蓄積。是皆良吏也。得是人而用之，民生可蘇、盜賊可息、風俗可淳歟？古人未嘗借才于異代，今天下文武之士歲進幾千人，獨無是人出于其間歟？抑或有之而莫之用歟？此天下剥膚之弊，而廟堂之所欲聞者也。諸士子其縱言之，主司者為之達。
translation_en: …infantry at Zelu was acclaimed throughout the realm for his valor; the one who executed rebellious commanders at Shuofang brought the military commands to observe the law; the one who stationed troops at strategic points, dredged waterways, and established military agricultural colonies brought the Qiang and other non-Chinese peoples to submission or defeat. These were all renowned generals. If such men were found and employed, could the army’s spirit be revived, the treasury replenished, and discipline upheld? The governor of Shu Commandery honored ritual propriety and righteousness in his administration; the magistrate of Chaoge was praised by the people as divinely discerning; the one who encouraged farming and sericulture, emphasized livestock raising, and prohibited extravagance ensured that his commandery had reserves. These were all worthy officials. If such men were found and employed, could the people’s livelihood be restored, banditry ended, and customs made wholesome? The ancients never borrowed talent from another age. Today, several thousand civil and military candidates advance each year throughout the realm: can it be that no such men emerge among them? Or do they exist, but no one employs them? These are scourges that cut into the very flesh of the realm, and matters on which the imperial court wishes to hear. Let you candidates speak freely; the examination officials will convey your words to the court.

title: 嘉靖七年順天府鄉試錄
text:
第壹場
四書
在明明德在親民在止於至善知止而后
有定定而后能靜靜而后能安安而后
能慮慮而后能得
馬一龍
同考試官訓導何批孔門入德之次第
盡在此數言塲中作者簡則包括不盡長則冗
贅不式此作能約要語發揮其亦造道有得而
===
言之親切者與允宜錄式
同考試官助教薛批講至善處尤精切
得古人立教宗旨盖嘗究心於大學者
考試官右庶子方批語意精到取之
考試官右庶子韓批辭不費而意自完可錄
聖經歷言大學之道而原其所以造於道也盖
明明德新民止於至善大學之道備矣然其所
以造於道者亦惟知止以馴致乎能得之地耳
此曾子述孔子之言以垂訓也其意若曰所謂

First Session

Four Books

“[The Way] lies in illuminating luminous virtue, in loving the people, and in resting in the highest good. Only after knowing where to rest can one have a settled purpose; only after having a settled purpose can one be still; only after being still can one be at ease; only after being at ease can one deliberate; only after deliberating can one attain it.”

This composition develops the meaning in concise, essential language. Surely its author has himself gained something in approaching the Way and thus speaks of it with intimate understanding! It certainly deserves to be recorded as a model.”

Comment by Associate Examiner Xue, Instructor: “The discussion of the highest good is particularly precise and apt, grasping the fundamental purpose of the ancients in establishing their teaching. The author has evidently devoted careful thought to the Great Learning.”

title: 嘉靖七年順天府鄉試錄
text:
大學之道果何如哉誠以吾德本明也而吾自
昏之必因其所發而洗濯澡雪使虛靈之天昭
然而復明焉大學之道不在於明明德乎民德
本新也而民自汚之必因其固有而鼓舞作興
使習染之舊煥然而一新焉大學之道不在於
新民乎明德有極致之地也必求至於是而不
遷誠而無息斯已矣新民有一定之則也必求
造於此而不易純而不已斯已矣大學之道又
在止於至善焉夫明德新民固欲止於至善矣
===
然其所以然之故果何如哉蓋君子於至善之
地既真知而不惑然後於所向之途斯一定而
不易既定矣則無以動其心而能靜既靜矣則
無所擇於地而能安夫既能安吾知從容於辨
别之頃而凡事之來處之精矣夫既能慮吾知
脫悟於精微之境而至善之理得之真矣是則
不止於至善無以成明德新民之功欲止於至
善必先知知止能得之序歸宿有其地造詣有
其方此所以為大學之道也歟抑論之聖人之

大學之道果何如哉？誠以吾德本明也，而吾自昏之，必因其所發而洗濯澡雪，使虛靈之天昭然而復明焉。大學之道不在於明明德乎？民德本新也，而民自汚之，必因其固有而鼓舞作興，使習染之舊煥然而一新焉。大學之道不在於新民乎？明德有極致之地也，必求至於是而不遷，誠而無息斯已矣；新民有一定之則也，必求造於此而不易，純而不已斯已矣。大學之道又在止於至善焉。夫明德新民，固欲止於至善矣，然其所以然之故，果何如哉？蓋君子於至善之地，既真知而不惑，然後於所向之途，斯一定而不易。既定矣，則無以動其心而能靜；既靜矣，則無所擇於地而能安。夫既能安，吾知從容於辨别之頃，而凡事之來，處之精矣。夫既能慮，吾知脫悟於精微之境，而至善之理，得之真矣。是則不止於至善，無以成明德新民之功；欲止於至善，必先知知止能得之序。歸宿有其地，造詣有其方，此所以為大學之道也歟？

抑論之，聖人之
translation_en:
…What, indeed, is the Way of the Great Learning? Our virtue is originally luminous, yet we ourselves obscure it. We must therefore take its manifestations as the starting point for cleansing and purifying it, so that the innate endowment of our empty and numinous mind shines forth and becomes luminous once more. Does not the Way of the Great Learning consist in making luminous virtue shine forth? The people’s virtue is originally fresh, yet they themselves defile it. We must therefore build upon what they inherently possess, encouraging and stirring them to action, so that the old accretions of habit are transformed into radiant newness. Does not the Way of the Great Learning consist in renewing the people? Making virtue luminous has an ultimate point of attainment: we must seek to reach it without departing from it, remaining sincere without interruption—that is all. Renewing the people has a fixed standard: we must seek to attain it without changing course, remaining pure without cease—that is all. The Way of the Great Learning also consists in resting in the highest good.

Making virtue luminous and renewing the people certainly aim at resting in the highest good. But what, indeed, is the reason underlying this? Once the gentleman truly knows the highest good as his destination and is free from doubt, the course toward which he directs himself becomes settled and unchanging. Once settled, nothing can stir his mind, and he can become still. Once still, he can be at ease wherever he finds himself. Once he can be at ease, I know that he will discriminate with composure and handle precisely every affair that arises. Once he can deliberate, I know that he will attain liberating insight [?] into the most subtle realm and truly grasp the principle of the highest good. Thus, without resting in the highest good, one cannot accomplish the work of making virtue luminous and renewing the people. To rest in the highest good, one must first understand the sequence leading from knowing where to rest to being able to attain it. There is a destination at which to arrive, and a method by which to advance. Is this not what constitutes the Way of the Great Learning?

translation_en:
…Way consists simply in illuminating luminous virtue and renewing the people; the highest good denotes their consummation. Why, then, does the Great Learning set these three expressions side by side? During the Spring and Autumn period, scholars did not understand the greatness of our learning and generally contented themselves with what was lowly and near at hand. They regarded the virtue of refinement and single-mindedness, and the transforming influence manifested in activity and change, as something as unattainable as divine intelligence. Thus the sage prominently set these before people. Yet he also feared that people would regard them as too lofty and fail to recognize the gateway to entering virtue. He therefore spoke further of knowing where to rest and being able to attain it.

不足以盡人而亦可以觀人吾於适蓋有取焉

translation_en:
…when the question was asked, but praised him after he had left. His meaning was this: “Although words cannot reveal everything about a person, they can nevertheless provide insight into him. In Kuo, I find something worthy of approval. As for a gentleman, I have often lamented that I could not meet one. Kuo deeply despises Yi and Ao, while honoring Yu and Ji. Judging his character by this, I know that he possesses outstanding discernment and does not blindly follow the times; he maintains an independent integrity and is not altered by prevailing customs. He perceives the Way clearly and believes in it firmly. On the strength of his attainments, he may be counted among the followers of the sages. He is unlike those in the world whose understanding is base. What a gentleman this man is! I have often thought that those who understand virtue are few. Kuo alone honors Yu and Ji, while rejecting Yi and Ao. Judging his heart by this, I know that his love of excellent virtue is rooted in the goodness of his innate moral nature, and that his attachment to noble honors arises from his heart’s desire [?]. He is exacting in his choices and correct in his aspirations. Examining what he holds within, one finds nothing but a sincere delight in goodness. He differs from those in the world whose aims are mean and low. How this man esteems virtue!”

Ah! In recognizing the man’s worth on the strength of his good words, the Master must have been moved by something here! At that time, the three Huan lineages usurped authority, and their power was formidable. Despite his sagely virtue, Confucius could obtain no position. Nangong Kuo, also known as Nan Rong, intended precisely to deplore prevailing ways and exalt the Master. There was indeed something difficult to answer in his words. Yet by waiting until he had left and then praising him, the Master gave him a profound answer. Before long, the descendants of the three Huan lineages declined. Great indeed is the Master! text:
際或能强制其心時乎富貴則氣盈而僭踰陵
縱將無不至焉能不淫乎大丈夫者雖享重禄
而敬畏之念恒存處高位而盈滿之懼方切不
驕也亦不侈也此心之定止水之澄也仁義禮
固行於富貴矣心何有於蕩邪常情於有餘之
地或能矜持其節時乎貧賤則氣歉而苟且放
溢將靡不為焉能不移乎大丈夫者雖終身屢
空而得之非道不苟取遯世不知而榮以非義
不苟受不諂也亦不援也一節之堅介石之固
===
也仁義禮固行於貧賤矣節何有於變邪至於
威武者人所甚畏也常人之情平居則悻戾自
高變故則惴懼失措矣大丈夫方且廣居居之
正位立之大道行之生死决於須臾也浩然之
氣不因之而或餒榮辱生於造次也毅然之色
不因之而或沮平生所存期於必伸矣孰得而
挫之哉夫士之處世富貴遇也貧賤常也威武
變也三者得而立身之道備矣非大丈夫安能
與於此嗟夫戰國之時聖賢道否天下不復見

translation_en:
…at such a juncture, they may manage to restrain their hearts forcibly. Yet when wealth and rank arrive, their spirits swell, and they transgress their bounds, becoming overbearing and unrestrained, stopping at nothing. How can they avoid being corrupted? A great man, however, though enjoying a substantial stipend, always retains a sense of reverence and caution; though occupying high office, he keenly fears the complacency of success. He is neither arrogant nor extravagant. His heart is as settled as still water is clear. Benevolence, righteousness, and ritual propriety are indeed practiced amid wealth and rank: how could his heart go astray? Ordinary people, when they have more than enough, may manage to maintain their integrity. Yet when poverty and low station arrive, their spirits falter, and they resort to expediency and abandon restraint, leaving nothing undone. How can they avoid wavering? A great man, however, though repeatedly destitute throughout his life, will not casually take anything acquired by improper means; though living in retirement, unknown to the world, he will not casually accept honors conferred unrighteously. He neither flatters nor seeks powerful support. The firmness of his integrity is the solidity of rock. Benevolence, righteousness, and ritual propriety are indeed practiced amid poverty and low station: how could his integrity change?

As for armed might, this is something people greatly fear. Ordinary people are obstinate and self-important in peaceful times, but tremble and lose their composure when upheaval comes. The great man, however, dwells in the spacious dwelling, stands in the correct position, and walks the great Way. Though life or death is decided in an instant, his vast, flowing vital force does not thereby falter; though honor or disgrace arises in a moment, his resolute countenance does not thereby lose heart. What he has upheld throughout his life he is determined to see prevail: who could thwart him? For a scholar living in the world, wealth and rank are a matter of opportunity, poverty and low station are the ordinary condition, and armed might is an extraordinary trial. If he handles all three rightly, his way of establishing himself is complete. Who but a great man could attain this? Alas! In the Warring States period, the Way of the sages and worthies was obstructed, and the world no longer witnessed…

Is this merely to make them wealthy and eminent? It is how he fulfills the requirements of ritual courtesy toward them. The sage makes nourishing the worthy his concern because he wishes them to extend this intention to the people. Once the worthy have received his support, they will surely carry this same concern over to others. In everything that can bring peace and relief to our people, they exhaust every means, so that the teeming population, well fed and warmly clothed, may all enjoy what brings them joy and benefit from what benefits them. Though the sage has never bestowed gifts on every household or enriched each person individually, whose blessings are not the beneficent influence of the sage reaching them? In everything that can sustain and nourish our people, the worthy leave no proper means untried, so that the countless multitudes may support their parents above and nurture their children below, each caring for their aged and tending their young. Though the sage has never distributed provisions morning and evening, where is his concern not universally present? Thus we know that the sage’s nourishing of the worthy is precisely his means of nourishing the people. How vast is the Way of nourishing!

人維新之治天下知所勸矣而出於神化之妙
焉則豈有不利者哉粤昔黃帝堯舜三聖迭興
知太朴之當變也而通之以禮義之俗修道立
教以新天下之耳目焉知草昧之將變也而通
之以文明之治制禮作樂以關天下之心志焉
由是斯世斯民鼓舞踴躍舍其舊而趨乎新者
終身由之而忘其勞也提撕警覺感於上而應
punctuated:
漢唐諸君，則其心私而政異，此又不可不察也。

「通其變，使民不倦；神而化之，使民宜之。」
樊深

同考試官教諭李批：講通變神化最是，且筆力老健，結處尤有見識。
同考試官署員外鄧批：寫出聖人通變神化之妙，若親際而見之，必達於治道者。

考試官右庶子韓批：渾厚典則，宜錄。

聖人新制作以勸天下，妙制作以利天下。夫聖人維新之治，天下知所勸矣，而出於神化之妙焉，則豈有不利者哉？粤昔黄帝、堯、舜，三聖迭興，知太朴之當變也，而通之以禮義之俗，修道立教，以新天下之耳目焉；知草昧之將變也，而通之以文明之治，制禮作樂，以開天下之心志焉。由是斯世斯民，鼓舞踴躍，舎其舊而趨乎新者，終身由之而忘其勞也；提撕警覺，感於上而應
translation_en:
…when practiced by the rulers of the Han and Tang, however, their intentions were selfish and their governance differed. This, too, must be carefully examined.

“Carry through changes so that the people do not grow weary; transform them with spiritual efficacy so that the people find what suits them.”
Fan Shen

Associate Examiner Li, Instructor, comments: “The explanation of carrying through changes and spiritually efficacious transformation is especially sound. Moreover, the writing is seasoned and vigorous, and the conclusion displays particular insight.”
Associate Examiner Deng, Acting Vice Director, comments: “He depicts the marvel of the sages’ carrying through changes and spiritually efficacious transformation as though he had personally encountered and witnessed it. He must be someone who comprehends the Way of governance.”
Examiner Fang, Right Vice Mentor, comments: “The atmosphere of the age of Tang Yao and Yu Shun and earlier times stands vividly before our eyes.”
Examiner Han, Right Vice Mentor, comments: “Substantial, ample, and conforming to classical standards. It merits selection.”

The sages renew institutions to encourage all under Heaven, and make their institutions wondrously effective to benefit all under Heaven. Under the sages’ renewing governance, all under Heaven know what should inspire their efforts. And when this governance proceeds through the marvel of spiritually efficacious transformation, how could anyone fail to benefit?

Long ago, the Yellow Emperor, Yao, and Shun—the three sages—arose in succession. Knowing that primordial simplicity ought to change, they carried that change through by establishing customs of ritual propriety and righteousness. They cultivated the Way and established instruction, renewing what all under Heaven heard and saw. Knowing that the age of uncultivated obscurity was about to change, they carried that change through by establishing enlightened governance. They instituted rites and created music, opening the minds and aspirations of all under Heaven.

Thus the people of that age were inspired and exhilarated. Those who abandoned the old and turned toward the new followed it throughout their lives, forgetting their toil. Roused and awakened, moved by those above and responding…

title: 嘉靖七年順天府鄉試錄
text:
於下者中心樂之而忘其倦也其天機之自動
殆若有以使之然乎然其所以通變者順其勢
之自然而不假於驅迫猶天運神道以司化權
盖有不疾而速者矣趣其時之適然而不由於
勉强猶地載神氣以成化功盖有不見而章者
矣由是斯世斯民利用以出利用以入而不以
爲難皞皞乎順帝之則而已左焉宜之右焉宜
之而莫知其故蕩蕩乎遵王之路而已其天理
之自孚亦若有以使之然乎吁聖人更化善治
===
如此其有功於天下大矣雖然變者聖人不得
已而用之也故變不欲驟驟則民駭而不安變
不欲强强則民苦而難入獨不觀之易道乎陽
窮於九必自少陰以趨六陰窮於六必自少陽
以趨九其來也有漸故其運也不息君子體乎
易道斯可以言治道矣

於下者，中心樂之而忘其倦也。其天機之自動，殆若有以使之然乎？然其所以通變者，順其勢之自然而不假於驅迫，猶天運神道以司化權，盖有不疾而速者矣；趣其時之適然而不由於勉强，猶地載神氣以成化功，盖有不見而章者矣。由是斯世斯民，利用以出，利用以入，而不以爲難，皞皞乎順帝之則而已；左焉宜之，右焉宜之，而莫知其故，蕩蕩乎遵王之路而已。其天理之自孚，亦若有以使之然乎？吁！聖人更化善治如此，其有功於天下大矣！雖然，變者聖人不得已而用之也。故變不欲驟，驟則民駭而不安；變不欲强，强則民苦而難入。獨不觀之易道乎？陽窮於九，必自少陰以趨六；陰窮於六，必自少陽以趨九。其來也有漸，故其運也不息。君子體乎易道，斯可以言治道矣。

四海之内咸仰朕德，時乃風。

translation_en:
…those below who respond rejoice in their hearts and forget their weariness. Does not this spontaneous stirring of their innate impulses seem as though something were making it so? Yet the sages adapt to change by following the natural course of circumstances, without resorting to coercion, just as Heaven employs its wondrous Way to wield the power of transformation: there is indeed speed without haste. They act in accordance with what the moment requires, without forcing matters, just as Earth bears the numinous vital force to accomplish transformation: there is indeed manifestation without being seen. Thus the people of this age benefit in going out and coming in, finding no difficulty in either; in simple contentment, they merely follow the Supreme Lord’s rule. Whether turning left or right, they find everything fitting, without knowing why; freely and expansively, they merely follow the king’s road. Does not this spontaneous realization of Heaven’s principle likewise seem as though something were making it so? Ah! Such are the sages’ transformation of customs and excellence in government: great indeed is their contribution to the world!
Nevertheless, change is something the sages employ only when they cannot do otherwise. Change should therefore not be sudden: suddenness frightens the people and unsettles them. Nor should change be forced: force makes the people suffer and renders it difficult for them to embrace it. Can we not see this in the Way of the Changes? When yang reaches its limit at nine, it must proceed through young yin toward six; when yin reaches its limit at six, it must proceed through young yang toward nine. Because its advent is gradual, its movement never ceases. Only by embodying the Way of the Changes can the gentleman speak of the Way of governing.
Book of Documents
“When all within the Four Seas look up to my virtue, this will be through your transforming influence.”
Qian Xuan

text:
同考試官訓導何批高宗於傅說望之
切故美之至子能發揮之曲盡其意有如在當
時者敬羡敬羡
同考試官助教薛批此作以務學法祖

考試官右庶子韓批氣象似此題
賢王以天下之望歸大臣之教蓋君得臣而萬
化行也大臣論學於上而天下仰德於下宜矣
===
此高宗所以美之也其意若曰君德係天下之
治忽相道係人主之得失朕之弗類何有於德
也今仰朕德者囿天下而一心蓋冀有以見乎
大有為之治朕之罔顯誠蔑于德也今望朕德
者合四海而同志蓋幸有以遇夫不世出之主
謂朕必至于罔覺而唐虞雍熙之化可復見于
當時矣謂朕必至于無愆而祖宗輯寧之功必
中興于今日矣若此者果何所致哉誠以說也
拔于傅巖而任之師保之官所以啓朕心者一

Comment by Associate Examiner He, Instructor: Gaozong’s expectations of Fu Yue were earnest, and so his praise was unstinting. You have developed this fully, bringing out every nuance of his meaning, as though you had been present at the time. Admirable, admirable!

Comment by Associate Examiner Xue, Assistant Instructor: This composition opens its exposition with diligent learning and emulation of the ancestors. Its language and meaning are earnest and thorough, vividly conveying Gaozong’s ardent expectations of Fu Yue.

Comment by Examiner Fang, Right Supervisor of Instruction: Upright and grand, lucid and vigorous.

Comment by Examiner Han, Right Supervisor of Instruction: Its spirit accords with this topic.

The worthy king attributed the hopes that all under Heaven placed in him to his great minister’s instruction. For when a ruler finds the right minister, the myriad transforming influences take effect. The great minister discusses learning with his sovereign above, while all under Heaven look up to the sovereign’s virtue below: this is fitting indeed. This was why Gaozong praised him. His meaning was as follows:

“The ruler’s virtue determines whether all under Heaven enjoy order or suffer disorder; the minister’s way determines the sovereign’s successes and failures. Unworthy as I am, what virtue do I possess? Yet now those who look up to my virtue embrace all under Heaven and are united in purpose, hoping thereby to witness a reign of great accomplishment. Lacking distinction, I am indeed deficient in virtue. Yet now those who place their hopes in my virtue join together throughout the Four Seas with a common aspiration, hoping for the good fortune of encountering a ruler such as rarely appears in the world.

“They believe that I will surely attain freedom from error, so that the harmonious and flourishing transformation wrought under Tang Yao and Yu Shun may be seen again in this age. They believe that I will surely become free from faults, so that the ancestors’ achievement of bringing concord and peace will assuredly be revived today. What, indeed, has brought this about? Truly, it is because Yue was raised from Fu Yan and appointed to the office of Mentor and Guardian. The means by which he enlightens my mind are all…”

title: 嘉靖七年順天府鄉試錄
text:
皆性命之懿足以動天下之聽聞求之形象而
授以冢宰之位所以訓朕志者莫非道德之純
足以起四海之景慕帝王之學不講也久矣學
於古訓之言出乎身即加乎民有不行而至之
神也若曰朕之恭默此憂居耳何足以致天下
之仰哉祖宗之法不振也久矣監于成憲之論
發乎邇即見乎遠有不疾而速之妙也若曰甘
盤之教此潛邸耳何足以致天下之仰哉若此
者非說之風而將誰歸也然則說也其思所以
===
俾朕副天下之望乎抑考高宗之初有商承平
日久成湯之道衰矣一旦高宗恭默思道起傅
說于築巖之下置之大臣之位君臣相勉宛然
都俞之風四海之中得不感動而仰望之乎高
宗此言雖所以美說然其責望之意已隱然溢
于言表矣故下文曰良臣惟聖
皇極之敷言是彝是訓于帝其訓
周良

皆性命之懿，足以動天下之聽聞。求之形象而授以冢宰之位，所以訓朕志者莫非道德之純，足以起四海之景慕。帝王之學不講也久矣，學於古訓之言，出乎身即加乎民，有不行而至之神也。若曰朕之恭默，此憂居耳，何足以致天下之仰哉？祖宗之法不振也久矣，監于成憲之論，發乎邇即見乎遠，有不疾而速之妙也。若曰甘盤之教，此潛邸耳，何足以致天下之仰哉？若此者非說之風而將誰歸也？然則說也，其思所以俾朕副天下之望乎？抑考高宗之初，有商承平日久，成湯之道衰矣。一旦高宗恭默思道，起傅說于築巖之下，置之大臣之位，君臣相勉，宛然都俞之風，四海之中得不感動而仰望之乎？高宗此言雖所以美說，然其責望之意已隱然溢于言表矣。故下文曰：「良臣惟聖。」

皇極之敷言，是彝是訓，于帝其訓。
周良

translation_en:
…all concern the excellence of human nature and Heaven’s mandate, sufficient to stir all who hear them throughout the realm. Having sought him by means of a portrait and appointed him Grand Steward, I find that everything with which he instructs my purpose embodies the purity of the Way and virtue, sufficient to inspire admiration throughout the Four Seas. The learning of emperors and kings has long gone unexamined. His counsel to learn from ancient teachings proceeds from my own person and extends immediately to the people, possessing the marvelous power of arriving without traveling. If one speaks of my reverent silence, that was merely my retirement in mourning: how could it suffice to win the admiration of all under Heaven? The laws of our ancestors have long gone unenforced. His counsel to examine established statutes issues from what is near and manifests itself in what is distant, possessing the subtle efficacy of achieving speed without haste. If one speaks of Gan Pan’s instruction, that belonged merely to my residence before accession: how could it suffice to win the admiration of all under Heaven? If such results are not due to Yue’s influence, to whom should they be attributed? Then, Yue, will you consider how to enable me to fulfill the hopes of all under Heaven?

Now, examining the beginning of Gaozong’s reign, we find that the Shang had long enjoyed peace, and the Way of Cheng Tang had declined. When Gaozong, in reverent silence, contemplated the Way, he raised Fu Yue from his wall-building beneath the cliffs and placed him among the high ministers. Ruler and minister encouraged one another, vividly recalling the harmonious exchanges of assent between ancient sage rulers and their ministers. Could those within the Four Seas fail to be moved and look up to them with hope? Although these words of Gaozong praise Yue, the expectations he placed upon him already emerge implicitly beyond the words themselves. Thus the following passage says: “A good minister makes his ruler a sage.”

The Sovereign’s Ultimate Standard, proclaimed in words, is the constant rule and the instruction; it is instruction from the Lord on High.
Zhou Liang

何其切乎戒以偏黨反側矣曰蕩蕩平平正直
歸其極焉丁寧更互以為說也感發何其至乎
皇極之敷言如此彼荒唐隱僻者異端之術耳

君子於王者至要之教，而深賛其妙也。盖王者感化斯民，其教莫要於敷言也，是宜君子有以深賛其妙焉。昔箕子告武王之意若曰：建天下之極，固在於君身；納天下於極，尤在於敷言。彼極乃天下之至理也，人君以之而著於章句之間，禁其私也，而又申其勸勉之意；極乃天下所取正也，人君以之而協於聲音之際，叙其詳也，而又總其通會之要。戒以偏陂好惡矣，曰王義、王道、王路，會其極焉，反覆推衍以為言也，鼓舞何其切乎！戒以偏黨反側矣，曰蕩蕩、平平、正直，歸其極焉，丁寧更互以為說也，感發何其至乎！皇極之敷言如此，彼荒唐隱僻者，異端之術耳。
translation_en:
…section, and the meaning of the commentary is very clear. Most writers fail to explain it fully. This essay alone singles out the two words “standard” and “promulgate”; its wording is precise, apt, classically grounded, and elegant. It can serve as a model for writers.
Associate Examiner Xue, Instructor, comments: The previously printed version only introduces “the king’s Way” and “the king’s righteousness” at the passage about Heaven’s instruction—a serious error. This composition gets it right, and therefore has been selected for inclusion.
Examiner Fang, Right Mentor, comments: Upright, grand, and in accord with classical norms, it can serve as a model.
Examiner Han, Right Mentor, comments: According to Cai’s Commentary, this is indeed the meaning.
The noble man deeply praises the subtle excellence of the king’s most essential teaching. For when a king influences and transforms the people, nothing in his teaching is more essential than promulgating his words. It is fitting, then, that the noble man should deeply praise their subtle excellence. The purport of what Jizi formerly told King Wu was as follows: Establishing the standard for all under Heaven certainly rests with the ruler’s own person; bringing all under Heaven into conformity with that standard depends especially upon promulgating his words. That standard is the supreme principle of all under Heaven. The ruler sets it forth in clauses and sentences, restraining the people’s selfishness while also elaborating his exhortations and encouragement. The standard is what all under Heaven look to for rectitude. The ruler gives it harmonious expression in sounds, setting out its particulars while also drawing together the essentials that unite them. He warns against deviation and partiality, against personal likes and dislikes; he speaks of “the king’s righteousness,” “the king’s Way,” and “the king’s road,” bringing them together in the standard. He develops these points repeatedly in his words: how earnestly he inspires the people! He warns against partisanship and perversity; he speaks of being “broad and open,” “level and even,” and “correct and straight,” bringing them back to the standard. He explains earnestly, varying and repeating his formulations: how profoundly he moves and awakens the people! Such is the promulgation of words concerning the August Standard. As for teachings that are fanciful, obscure, and abstruse, these are merely the methods of heterodox schools.

translation_en:
…Are these proclaimed words not the constant principles of all under Heaven? They concern the pressing duties of everyday life and the enduring human relationships: the plain and accessible Way of centrality and constancy, which sage and ordinary man alike can practice. What is crooked, deviant, narrow, or petty is merely a one-sided doctrine. Are these proclaimed words not the great instruction for all under Heaven? They constitute the great canon for establishing rules and handing down models—an exposition of what is luminous, upright, and great, which all under Heaven cannot alter through ten thousand generations. Though the instruction is proclaimed by the ruler, its principles are Heaven’s ordering and Heaven’s arrangement. The ruler merely serves Heaven; what, then, could this be but Heaven’s instruction? Though the ruler elaborates the instruction, his words accord wholly with Heaven and convey Heaven’s meaning. The ruler merely acts on Heaven’s behalf; again, what could this be but Heaven’s instruction? The Supreme Standard is rooted in Heaven; the people receive Heaven’s principles; and the ruler is one who has attained them first. By means of the Heaven within himself, he moves the Heaven within the people’s hearts. Surely it is fitting that the people should turn to the Supreme Standard!

Ah! Reading the section on the Supreme Standard, one understands the ancients’ intention in teaching. They grounded it in establishing the Supreme Standard, followed this with methods of cultivating people, and completed it with the instruction of proclaimed words. Thus people could calmly immerse themselves in and savor it, entering into it unawares. In later ages, teaching by personal example and teaching through rules have sometimes approximated this, but teaching through poetry has ceased. How difficult, then, to hope for the good government of the ancients!

其旋元吉之休自見於服飾言之大帶垂於身
物雖輕矣而矩法之所關者重可以覘夫人之
所養也人豈無失其常乎我君子動必由禮而
其帶則伊絲焉真素為質用崇沖澹之體雜采
為文畧施藻飾之華蓋先王之法服自有常度
亦惟遵之而已曷嘗踰矩以立異哉皮弁戴於
首物雖小矣而繩規之所係者嚴可以窺夫人
之所守也人豈無忒其度乎我君子之帶伊絲

translation_en:
…the blessing of supreme good fortune in his return. Consider how this manifests itself in his attire. The great sash hangs from his body: though the object is light, the standards involved are weighty, and through it one can discern what a man has cultivated within himself. Are there not people who depart from the constant standard? Our gentleman invariably acts according to ritual, and his sash is of silk. Plain, undyed silk forms its substance, honoring an unassuming simplicity; assorted colors form its pattern, adding only a little ornamental splendor. The prescribed robes of the former kings have their constant standards, and he merely follows them. When has he ever overstepped the rules to make himself different?

The leather cap is worn upon his head: though the object is small, the rules governing it are strict, and through it one can perceive what a man holds fast to. Are there not people who deviate from the proper measure? Our gentleman’s sash is of silk, and his cap is dark greenish-black. Its appearance rises prominently, its hue a pure dark greenish-black; its form stands lofty, its color matching that of a fine horse. The rites established by the sages have their fixed forms, and he merely conforms to them. When has he ever exceeded the prescribed design and contravened the enduring norms? Thus, constancy in attire expresses unity in his deportment. And what is unity in deportment if not unity of heart? The poet indeed knew well how to praise his gentleman!

Yet, considering this poem in the Airs of Cao, was the gentleman of whom it speaks truly a worthy man of settled judgment and steadfast resolve? Otherwise, why repeatedly praise his single-minded constancy without cease? Could he have been someone like the grand master Xi Fuji 羖負羈 [?]? I fear that even his worthiness would not suffice to merit such words. Alas! The state lacked the gathering clouds rising in the morning [?]. Were such a man to encounter an enlightened age, his talents and plans for setting the four quarters right could surely do more than merely transform the ways depicted in “The Mayfly.” By employing him, one might hope to bring a transforming influence to all under Heaven!

不修矣衛武公作詩使人日誦以自警者如此
意謂爾欲君德之修亦必先爲之地可焉何則
豈弟可即而復謙之卑和慎可親而居巽之順

translation_en:
“Gentle and reverent is the man: this is the foundation of virtue. If he is a wise man, tell him words of good counsel, and he will follow the practice of virtue.”
Tian Ze
Comment by Associate Examiner Zhang, Assistant Instructor: Humility nurtures virtue; discernment welcomes admonition. This expresses Duke Wu’s intention to advance tirelessly in virtue. This essay is dignified and mature, as though spoken by the poet himself. You, too, are someone with whom one may discuss the Odes.
Comment by Associate Examiner Li, Instructor: Writing that explains principles should certainly not prize superficial generalities. This work is gentle in spirit and elegant in diction, wholly as though naturally formed. Hearing his words, might its author also be a reverent and wise scholar?
Comment by Associate Examiner Fang, Secretary: The two occurrences of “virtue” refer distinctly to the mind and to personal conduct, deriving from “reverent” and “wise” above [?]. This work fully realizes its meaning and is precise in expression: the writing of a seasoned hand.
Comment by Examiner Fang, Right Vice Mentor: Pure and elegant.
Comment by Examiner Han, Right Vice Mentor: Clear, fluent, skillful, and finely wrought. An excellent work.
The reverent man grounds himself in goodness; the wise man receives goodness. This is the worthy lord’s intention in admonishing himself. Goodness is the substance of virtue. When the reverent man grounds himself in goodness and the wise man empties himself to receive it, no aspect of virtue goes uncultivated. Such was the purpose of Duke Wu of Wei in composing a poem and having others recite it daily to admonish him. Its meaning is this: if you wish to cultivate the virtue of a ruler, you must first prepare a foundation for it. Why? Being amiable and approachable, one then assumes the lowly position of humility [?]; being harmonious, cautious, and easy to draw near to, one abides in the yielding disposition of deference …

title: 嘉靖七年順天府鄉試錄
text:
是温温恭人也資稟本于天賦之良志氣得于
涵養之漸德不自此而可進耶但見暴戾消而
性不鑿真源凝靜悠然日趨於義理之奥也傲
惰去而心無僻思慮沉潜駸乎上達於性天之
蘊也盖善無常主一德之至胥此乎基恭之裨
於德深矣爾無為恭乎至若離照中含而炳物
之幾晉明自昭而見事之賾是謂哲人也密察
足以别乎視聽疏通足以審乎容納言之而豈
有不受耶但見有物有恒古者言行兼謹之善
===
言也告之遂踐其實一維樞機之是慎焉制事
制心古者動靜交修之德言也迪之即率于行
一維義禮之是順焉盖虛以受人衆善攸集德
斯不孤智之資於德大矣爾焉得為智乎噫武
公誦此自儆則必不矯亢以自高訑訑以拒人
者茲其德之所由懋歟抑嘗考之淇奧亦美武
公之德也切磋琢磨則知其無不受乎盡言金
錫圭璧正温恭之所鍛鍊以成焉者抑戒之誦
豈直託諸言已哉噫睿聖之學君人者之所當

translation_en: …Such is the gentle, reverent man. His natural endowment is rooted in the goodness bestowed by Heaven, and his resolve and vital spirit develop through gradual cultivation. Can virtue not advance from this foundation? One sees only that violence and perversity dissolve while his nature remains uninjured; its true source grows still and composed, and day by day he calmly approaches the depths of moral principle. Arrogance and indolence depart, leaving his mind free of deviation; his thoughts become profound and concentrated, advancing toward a higher understanding of the mysteries of his Heaven-given nature. Goodness has no fixed possessor: the perfection of unified virtue is founded entirely upon this. Reverence contributes profoundly to virtue. Will you not practice reverence? As for one who inwardly possesses the illumination of Li and thus discerns the subtle beginnings of things, whose brightness shines forth like Jin and thus perceives the intricacies of affairs—such a person is called wise. His close scrutiny suffices to distinguish what he sees and hears; his breadth of understanding suffices to judge what he should admit and accept. When words are offered to him, how could he fail to receive them? One sees that having substance in speech and constancy in conduct was the ancients’ sound teaching on exercising care in both word and deed. Once told this, he puts its substance into practice, attending carefully to words and deeds as the pivots of action. Regulating affairs and regulating the mind was the ancients’ teaching on virtue, on cultivating oneself in both activity and stillness. Once guided by this, he follows it in his conduct, adhering solely to righteousness and ritual propriety. By emptying oneself to receive others’ counsel, one gathers every kind of goodness, and virtue is no longer alone. Wisdom contributes greatly to virtue. How, then, may you become wise? Ah! Duke Wu recited this to admonish himself; surely he would neither exalt himself through obstinate pride nor reject others with smug complacency. Was this how his virtue came to flourish? Moreover, I have examined “The Recesses of the Qi” (Qi ao), which also praises Duke Wu’s virtue. Its references to cutting, filing, chiseling, and polishing show that he accepted all fully spoken counsel; its gold, tin, jade tablets, and jade discs represent precisely what his gentleness and reverence refined and brought to completion. Could his recitation of the admonitions in “Restraint” (Yi) have been merely a matter of words? Ah! The learning of the sagely wise is what those who rule over others ought to…

“In the ninth month, on dingmao, the son Tong was born.” Sixth year of Duke Huan. “The ruler of Wu sent Zha on a diplomatic visit.” Twenty-ninth year of Duke Xiang. “In the ninth month, on jihai, the duke fled to Qi.” Twenty-fifth year of Duke Zhao. “The men of Song seized the ruler of Xiao Zhu.” Fourth year of Duke Ai.

This essay deeply grasps their purport, and its prose is also classical and elegant. Its author evidently has profound learning in the Spring and Autumn Annals and fully deserves recommendation for a high place.”

Comment by Examiner Fang, Right Junior Mentor: “The language and reasoning are rigorous and orderly.”

Comment by Examiner Han, Right Junior Mentor: “Clear and fluent; worthy of selection.”

In revising the Classic, the Sage provided means to reveal the principles of hereditary succession and abdication, and means to weigh the proper balance between refinement and substance. Here we see that the Spring and Autumn Annals encompasses the Way of both the ancient emperors and the kings; none but a sage could have revised it. Displayed through actual events, are its teachings not profound, incisive, manifest, and clear? Now, the Spring and Autumn Annals was merely the history of Lu. How did Confucius’s revision make it encompass the Way of emperors and kings? Truly, the transfer and acceptance of rule over all under Heaven is a matter of the greatest importance: how could anyone dare treat it as a private possession? title: 嘉靖七年順天府鄉試錄
text:
禮舉之而國本于是乎定庶孽之生莫可匹矣
書之者與之也其以居正為大而不必於讓國
之義乎吳札聘魯黜而稱名若曰此吳賢公子
也當任家國之寄何潔身去之使國統于是乎
乖爭弑之禍其階之矣名之者貶之也其以達
節為權而不拘於世及之禮乎是則繼也禪也
惟其公也聖人何心哉所以示其法者如此若
夫世尚損益禮之大者其何可泥是故古尚質
而不諱周尚文而始諱其制殊也乃魯昭齊陽
===
州之奔特書曰孫蓋昭公魯祖也而可忘乎今
去社稷之奉則危辱之大者苟暴揚其事忠敬
之心薄矣惡乎訓故書孫者諱之也諱之者非
阿也放周之文而已宋景小邾子之執直書宋
人然定公宋名也而可犯乎蓋以臨文不諱寔
禮律所載者苟隱避其詞是非之迹泯矣惡乎
傳故書宋者不諱也不諱者非瀆也從古之質
而已是則文也質也唯其時也聖人何心哉所
以參其中者如此謂之兼帝王之道信哉吁繼

translation_en: …the rites were observed in celebrating his birth, and thereby the foundation of the state was secured; no son born to a concubine could rival him. Recording this signified approval. Was this not to place foremost the maintenance of the rightful position, without insisting upon the duty of yielding the state to another? When Zha of Wu visited Lu on a diplomatic mission, he was demoted in wording and called by his personal name, as though to say: “This is a worthy prince of Wu, who ought to have accepted responsibility for his ruling house and state. Why did he preserve his personal purity by withdrawing, thereby disrupting the succession and opening the way to the disasters of contention and regicide?” Naming him signified censure. Was this not to exercise discretion through a flexible understanding of moral obligations, without being bound by the ritual rules of hereditary succession? Thus, whether succession was hereditary or through abdication, what mattered was impartiality. What private preference could the sage have had? Such was his way of setting forth the governing rules. As for the additions and reductions made according to the preferences of successive ages, these are major matters of ritual: how could one cling rigidly to a single practice? Thus antiquity valued plainness and did not employ taboo avoidance, whereas the Zhou valued refinement and began to do so; their institutions differed. When Duke Zhao of Lu fled to Yangzhou in Qi, the record specifically used the word “withdrew” (sun 孫). Duke Zhao was an ancestral ruler of Lu: could this be forgotten? His departure from the service of the altars of soil and grain was a matter of utmost peril and humiliation. To expose the affair openly would weaken feelings of loyalty and reverence; how could that offer instruction? Thus writing “withdrew” concealed the disgrace. Such concealment was no flattery: it merely followed Zhou refinement. When Duke Jing of Song seized the Viscount of Xiaozhu, the record wrote straightforwardly, “the men of Song.” Yet Song was Duke Ding’s personal name: could its taboo be infringed? The rule that taboo avoidance does not apply when composing a text is indeed recorded in the ritual regulations. If the wording were concealed or avoided, the evidence of right and wrong would be effaced; how could it be transmitted? Thus writing “Song” dispensed with taboo avoidance. This was no disrespect: it merely followed the plainness of antiquity. Thus, whether refinement or plainness was employed depended upon the time. What private preference could the sage have had? Such was his way of weighing the two to attain the proper mean. How true it is to say that he combined the Way of the emperors and kings! Ah, hereditary succession…

行然後有嫡庶易位者矣然後有畀國匪人者
矣然後有犯上干主違禮獻佞者矣爭奪起而
禍變相尋國惡彰而名實紊亂可勝嘆哉
遂伐楚次于陘　楚屈完來盟于師盟于召
陵〔僖公四年〕宋人齊人楚人盟于鹿上
秋宋公楚子陳侯蔡侯鄭伯許男曹伯
會于盂　執宋公以伐宋〔僖公二十一年〕
===
創伯攘外而申尊王之義春秋之所褒繼伯交
考試官右庶子韓　批〔說出桓襄之功罪〕
考試官右庶子方　批〔得謹嚴體〕
用錄式
意旨而文且有則蓋學於春秋而知大義者是
楚以尊周室也宋襄不能得失自見此作獨得
爲本故予桓公之功稱管仲之仁者以其能攘
同考試官行人楊　批〔孔子作春秋以尊周〕

punctuated:
禪有法，則傳世之義明；文質得中，則經世之義正。此孔子脩經之功所以為大也與！唯此義不行，然後有嫡庶易位者矣，然後有畀國匪人者矣，然後有犯上干主、違禮獻佞者矣。爭奪起而禍變相尋，國惡彰而名實紊亂，可勝嘆哉！
「遂伐楚，次于陘。楚屈完來盟于師，盟于召陵。」僖公四年。「宋人、齊人、楚人盟于鹿上。秋，宋公、楚子、陳侯、蔡侯、鄭伯、許男、曹伯會于盂，執宋公以伐宋。」僖公二十一年。
同考試官行人楊批：孔子作《春秋》，以尊周為本，故予桓公之功、稱管仲之仁者，以其能攘楚以尊周室也。宋襄不能，得失自見。此作獨得意旨，而文且有則，蓋學於《春秋》而知大義者，是用錄式。

translation_en:
…when abdication follows established rules, the principle of transmitting rule to succeeding generations becomes clear; when refinement and substance attain their proper balance, the principle of ordering the world is set right. Is this not what makes Confucius’s achievement in editing the classic so great! Only when this principle is not observed do the legitimate heir and the sons of secondary wives exchange places, states get handed over to unworthy men, and men offend their superiors and defy their rulers, violating ritual propriety and offering flattery. Contention arises, disasters and upheavals follow one another, the evils of states are exposed, and names and realities fall into confusion. How could one lament this enough!
“They then attacked Chu and encamped at Xing. Qu Wan of Chu came to make a covenant with the army; they made the covenant at Shaoling.” Fourth year of Duke Xi. “Men of Song, Qi, and Chu made a covenant at Lushang. In autumn, the Duke of Song, the Viscount of Chu, the Marquis of Chen, the Marquis of Cai, the Earl of Zheng, the Baron of Xu, and the Earl of Cao met at Yu. They seized the Duke of Song and attacked Song.” Twenty-first year of Duke Xi.
Comment by Associate Examiner Yang, Messenger: Confucius composed the Spring and Autumn Annals with honoring Zhou as its foundation. Thus, he approved Duke Huan’s achievements and praised Guan Zhong’s benevolence because they were able to repel Chu and thereby honor the royal house of Zhou. Duke Xiang of Song could not do so; their respective successes and failures are self-evident. This composition alone grasps the purport, and its writing also follows proper standards. Its author is evidently someone who has studied the Spring and Autumn Annals and understood its great principles. It is therefore recorded as a model.
Comment by Examiner Fang, Right Mentor: It achieves a careful and rigorous style.
Comment by Examiner Han, Right Mentor: It brings out the achievements and faults of Dukes Huan and Xiang.
To establish the hegemony, repel outsiders, and uphold the principle of honoring the king is what the Spring and Autumn Annals praises; to succeed to the hegemony and enter into relations…

title: 嘉靖七年順天府鄉試錄
text:
外而乖尊王之義春秋之所貶夫伯者所以合
衆攘夷以尊王室者也齊桓伐楚而宋襄與之
會盟得失為何如哉觀春秋所書予奪之情見
矣且春秋何為而作也為尊周而作也是故齊
桓之主伯也楚人伐鄭合八國以討之于是乎
有陘亭之次焉屈完來師退召陵而與盟焉夫
桓專命興師何褒之有盖楚自東周以來僭稱
號而廢職貢無王巳乆不有以攘却之周其不
可為乎所幸桓也仗義執言聲罪致討責包茅
===
不貢也問王祭不共也遂使輸詞服罪遣使求
盟覬覦窺伺之心由是潜矣周之所以幸存誰
之力歟噫夾輔王室桓其率先職乎春秋書次
于陘楚屈完來盟于師盟于召陵序其績也非
以其申尊王之義邪迨夫宋襄之圖伯也諸侯
未孚邀楚子以求之于是乎有鹿上之盟焉楚
再會盂執宋公以伐宋焉夫襄自反而縮何貶
之為盖楚自桓公既沒朝諸侯而盟中國無王
□故使有以摧抑之周其猶有賴乎夫何襄也

punctuated: 外而乖尊王之義，春秋之所貶。夫伯者，所以合衆攘夷以尊王室者也。齊桓伐楚，而宋襄與之會盟，得失為何如哉？觀春秋所書，予奪之情見矣。且春秋何為而作也？為尊周而作也。是故齊桓之主伯也，楚人伐鄭，合八國以討之，于是乎有陘亭之次焉。屈完來，師退召陵而與盟焉。夫桓專命興師，何褒之有？盖楚自東周以來，僭稱號而廢職貢，無王巳乆。不有以攘却之，周其不可為乎？所幸桓也，仗義執言，聲罪致討，責包茅不貢也，問王祭不共也，遂使輸詞服罪，遣使求盟，覬覦窺伺之心由是潜矣。周之所以幸存，誰之力歟？噫！夾輔王室，桓其率先職乎？春秋書次于陘、楚屈完來盟于師、盟于召陵，序其績也，非以其申尊王之義邪？迨夫宋襄之圖伯也，諸侯未孚，邀楚子以求之，于是乎有鹿上之盟焉。楚再會盂，執宋公以伐宋焉。夫襄自反而縮，何貶之為？盖楚自桓公既沒，朝諸侯而盟中國，無王□故，使有以摧抑之，周其猶有賴乎？夫何襄也
translation_en:
…with outsiders, contravening the principle of honoring the king: this is what the Spring and Autumn Annals condemns. The hegemon’s function is to unite the many states and repel the barbarians in order to honor the royal house. Duke Huan of Qi attacked Chu, whereas Duke Xiang of Song met and covenanted with it. How should their successes and failures be judged? The grounds for approval and disapproval become apparent when we examine what the Spring and Autumn Annals records. Why, indeed, was the Spring and Autumn Annals written? It was written to uphold Zhou.

Thus, when Duke Huan of Qi presided as hegemon, the men of Chu attacked Zheng, and he united eight states to punish them. This led to the army’s encampment at Xingting. Qu Wan arrived, the army withdrew to Shaoling, and a covenant was concluded with him. Now Huan raised an army on his own authority: what was there to praise in this? Since the beginning of Eastern Zhou, Chu had usurped a royal title and discontinued its prescribed tribute; it had long disregarded the king. Without someone to repel it, could anything have been done for Zhou? Fortunately, Huan upheld righteousness and advanced a just cause, proclaimed Chu’s offenses and undertook a punitive expedition. He reproached it for failing to present tribute of bundled mao grass and questioned its failure to supply the royal sacrifices. He thereby made it offer a statement acknowledging guilt and send an envoy to seek a covenant. Its ambitions and watchful designs were consequently suppressed. By whose efforts did Zhou enjoy its fortunate survival? Ah! In supporting the royal house, did Huan not take the lead in fulfilling his duty? The Spring and Autumn Annals records the encampment at Xing, Qu Wan of Chu’s coming to covenant with the army, and the covenant at Shaoling, setting out his achievements. Was this not because he upheld the principle of honoring the king?

When Duke Xiang of Song sought hegemony, however, he had not won the trust of the other lords, so he invited the Viscount of Chu in pursuit of it. This led to the covenant at Lushang. Chu met with them again at Yu, seized the Duke of Song, and attacked Song. Now, if Xiang examined himself and found himself upright, why condemn him? Since Duke Huan’s death, Chu had received the other lords at its court and bound the central states in covenants, disregarding the king [text unclear: □故]. Had someone checked and restrained it, would Zhou not still have had someone to rely upon? How was it, then, that Xiang…

title: 嘉靖七年順天府鄉試錄
text:
既與之盟復與之會决內外之防也昧膺懲之
訓也卒致身為夷俘國遭塗炭跋扈陸梁之勢
于焉熾矣周之所以不振誰之過與噫作賓王
家襄其忝厥祖乎春秋人宋公于鹿上之盟而
盂之會直書其事而不隱深貶之也非以其乖
尊王之義邪吁攘夷以尊王者特褒其不能者
加貶春秋之義明矣夷夏君臣之際嚴矣抑宋
襄無足道者若首止之定儲葵丘之明禁則齊
桓尊周不特攘楚而已雖然桓公之功管仲佐
===
之也然亦假之而已管仲死而伯業衰矣宋之
子魚亦齊之管仲也何得失之殊邪噫諫不行
言不聽有賢與無賢等耳君人者鑒諸
禮記
是故昔先王之制禮也因其財物而致其
義焉爾故作大事必順天時為朝夕必
放於日月為高必因丘陵為下必因川
澤是故天時雨澤君子達亹亹焉
陳時

punctuated:
既與之盟，復與之會，决內外之防也，昧膺懲之訓也。卒致身為夷俘，國遭塗炭，跋扈陸梁之勢于焉熾矣。周之所以不振，誰之過與？噫！作賓王家，襄其忝厥祖乎！春秋人宋公于鹿上之盟，而盂之會直書其事而不隱，深貶之也，非以其乖尊王之義邪？吁！攘夷以尊王者特褒，其不能者加貶，春秋之義明矣，夷夏君臣之際嚴矣。抑宋襄無足道者，若首止之定儲、葵丘之明禁，則齊桓尊周不特攘楚而已。雖然，桓公之功，管仲佐之也，然亦假之而已。管仲死而伯業衰矣。宋之子魚亦齊之管仲也，何得失之殊邪？噫！諫不行，言不聽，有賢與無賢等耳。君人者鑒諸！
禮記
是故昔先王之制禮也，因其財物而致其義焉爾。故作大事必順天時，為朝夕必放於日月，為高必因丘陵，為下必因川澤。是故天時雨澤，君子達亹亹焉。
陳時
translation_en:
…Having already entered into a covenant with Chu, he then met with it again, breaching the boundary between the inner and outer realms and disregarding the injunction to chastise the unruly. In the end, he himself became a captive of the barbarians, his state suffered utter devastation, and their insolent, unbridled power thereby grew rampant. Whose fault was it that Zhou could not recover its strength? Alas! As a guest of the royal house, did Duke Xiang not disgrace his ancestors? At the covenant at Lushang, the Spring and Autumn Annals reduces the Duke of Song to the designation “man”; at the meeting at Yu, it records the affair directly, concealing nothing. This is profound censure. Is it not because he violated the principle of honoring the king? Ah! Those who repel the barbarians to honor the king receive special praise; those who fail to do so incur censure. The meaning of the Spring and Autumn Annals is clear, and the distinctions between barbarians and the Chinese, and between ruler and minister, are strictly maintained.
Yet Duke Xiang of Song scarcely merits discussion. As for settling the succession at Shouzhi and proclaiming prohibitions at Kuiqiu, Duke Huan of Qi’s honoring of Zhou went beyond merely repelling Chu. Even so, Duke Huan’s achievements depended on Guan Zhong’s assistance; he was, moreover, merely borrowing the principle of honoring the king for his own purposes. When Guan Zhong died, his hegemony declined. Ziyu of Song was also a counterpart to Guan Zhong of Qi: why were success and failure so different? Alas! When remonstrances are not acted upon and advice is not heeded, having a worthy adviser is no different from having none. Let those who rule others take warning from this!
Record of Rites
“Thus, when the former kings of antiquity established rites, they simply drew upon their material resources to give full expression to the appropriate meaning. Hence, in undertaking great affairs, they invariably followed Heaven’s seasons; in instituting morning and evening observances, they invariably modeled them on the sun and moon. In building on high ground, they invariably made use of hills and mounds; in building on low ground, they invariably made use of rivers and marshes. Thus, when Heaven sends seasonable rain and moisture, the gentleman brings his diligent endeavors to fruition.”
Chen Shi

title: 嘉靖七年順天府鄉試錄
text:
同考試官主事吳批題本明白作者類泥
傳註纏繞可厭此篇順題講去而於先王制禮
之意提撥明甚可佳
考試官右庶子方批不冗不泛
考試官右庶子韓批簡當可錄
論先王制禮因物而致義必詳其禮而原其意
焉盖物生於天地而禮所以定義也先王有感
於天地生物之功而用物以致義焉其心能自
已哉記禮器者謂夫無物不可以為禮而物者
===
禮之所資用物不可以無義而禮者義之定制
先王制為祭祀之禮亦惟因天地所生之財物
以致其用之之義焉爾何則運行莫大乎天時
也為郊雩之事則必順天時而行之期日之有
常焉著明莫大乎日月也為朝夕之祭則必放
日月而行之東西之有位焉為高上之祭於丘
陵以丘陵高而顯也為在下之祭於川澤以川
澤深而隱也因物致義之禮如此所以然者得
無意歟盖無時而或息者天地之化有感而必

Associate Examiner Wu, Secretary, comments: “The topic itself is clear, but writers generally cling to the commentaries, becoming tiresomely entangled in them. This essay follows the topic through its exposition and brings out very clearly the intention behind the former kings’ institution of ritual. It is commendable.”
Examiner Fang, Right Vice Supervisor of Instruction, comments: “Neither verbose nor vague.”
Examiner Han, Right Vice Supervisor of Instruction, comments: “Concise and apt; worthy of inclusion.”
In discussing how the former kings instituted ritual by drawing upon material things to give expression to what is right, one must examine their rites in detail and trace their underlying intention. Material things are produced by Heaven and Earth, while ritual establishes what is right. Moved by Heaven and Earth’s achievement in producing things, the former kings used those things to give expression to what is right. Could their hearts have restrained themselves? The author of Ritual Vessels says that there is nothing that cannot serve in ritual, and material things are the resources upon which ritual draws; material things cannot be used without regard to what is right, and ritual is the established form of what is right. In instituting sacrificial rites, the former kings likewise simply drew upon the resources produced by Heaven and Earth to give expression to the rightness of their use.
Why is this so? Among recurring movements, none is greater than the seasons of Heaven. Thus, in conducting the suburban sacrifices and sacrifices for rain, they necessarily followed Heaven’s seasons, with fixed dates for their observance. Among shining lights, none is greater than the sun and moon. Thus, in conducting the morning and evening sacrifices, they necessarily took the sun and moon as their model, with designated positions in the east and west. They performed sacrifices to those on high upon hills and mounds because hills and mounds are elevated and conspicuous; they performed sacrifices to those below at rivers and marshes because rivers and marshes are deep and hidden. Such were the rites that drew upon material things to give expression to what is right. Could there have been no intention underlying their being so? title: 嘉靖七年順天府鄉試錄
text:
通者君子之心皆天雨露之以時降也而既優
既渥盛大普徧於萬物君子則見夫天地之生

…that responds and achieves communion is the heart of the gentleman. Heaven’s rain and dew descend in their season [?], abundant and ample, spreading generously over all things. The gentleman thus perceives how Heaven and Earth bring things into being, nurturing their growth: their great virtue works tirelessly and without end. Seeing the achievement of Heaven and Earth in producing material resources, he is deeply moved within. How could he fail to use these resources to express his sincerity in requiting their source? Is this not why the former kings established rites that used material things to give expression to moral significance, and why the recorder set them down to instruct others? Yet, to pursue the matter further: great indeed is the achievement of Heaven and Earth. Examining another chapter, however, we also find: “Fewness is prized.” What does this mean? Confucius said: “Rites differ; neither lavishness nor sparseness is prescribed.” This means that each has what is appropriate to it. Nevertheless, in their essentials, all take sincerity and reverence as their foundation. The Book of Documents says: “Millet is not what gives fragrance; luminous virtue alone gives fragrance.”

title: 嘉靖七年順天府鄉試錄
text:
本天地之和序而作者也明於其本而禮樂有
不可興者哉樂記君子謂夫人知禮樂之作於
聖人而不知其原於天地何則氣行不乖而百
物皆化質具有秩而群物皆别此天地之和序
而禮樂所由始也聖人仰觀俯察以其心所存
主者而參之於天地陽動生物之機有得於運
旋不言之表神而明之盖非聞見之知也陰靜
成物之德妙契於昭著不動之餘感而通之固
有知化之神也如是而禮樂不可興乎誠以不
===
知而妄作者恒易以過過則暴亂之失不免而
禮樂所以不興也夫既明於天地則能以其心
所獨得者而見之於制作恊義以起所未有因
情而為之節文凡所以等貴賤定親疎者無非
散殊之義之所顯著序以贊序天地成物資之
矣夫奚至於過制而亂邪正律以和聲審音以
定樂凡所以格神人和上下者無非合同之化
之所昭宣和以敦和天地生物資之矣夫庸至
於過作而暴邪夫樂由天作必明於天地之和
