punctuated: 本天地之和序，而作者也明於其本，而禮樂有不可興者哉？《樂記》君子謂：夫人知禮樂之作於聖人，而不知其原於天地。何則？氣行不乖，而百物皆化；質具有秩，而群物皆别。此天地之和序，而禮樂所由始也。聖人仰觀俯察，以其心所存主者而參之於天地。陽動生物之機，有得於運旋不言之表，神而明之，盖非聞見之知也；陰靜成物之德，妙契於昭著不動之餘，感而通之，固有知化之神也。如是，而禮樂不可興乎？誠以不知而妄作者恒易以過，過則暴亂之失不免，而禮樂所以不興也。夫既明於天地，則能以其心所獨得者而見之於制作。恊義以起所未有，因情而為之節文，凡所以等貴賤、定親疎者，無非散殊之義之所顯著。序以贊序，天地成物資之矣，夫奚至於過制而亂邪？正律以和聲，審音以定樂，凡所以格神人、和上下者，無非合同之化之所昭宣。和以敦和，天地生物資之矣，夫庸至於過作而暴邪？夫樂由天作，必明於天地之和
translation_en:
…are grounded in the harmony and order of Heaven and Earth. Those who institute them understand their foundation; how, then, could rites and music fail to flourish? The gentleman in the Record of Music says: People know that rites and music were instituted by the sages, but do not know that they originate in Heaven and Earth. Why is this? Vital energy moves without discord, and the myriad things all undergo transformation; material forms possess an ordered arrangement, and all things are differentiated. This is the harmony and order of Heaven and Earth, from which rites and music originate.

The sage observes above and examines below, comparing what he holds and honors in his heart with Heaven and Earth. He apprehends the workings by which active yang generates things beyond their wordless revolutions, understanding them with spiritual insight: this is surely no knowledge acquired through hearing and sight. He accords wondrously with the potency by which still yin brings things to completion, beyond its manifest yet unmoving presence, responding to it and comprehending it: here indeed is the spiritual insight that knows transformation. With such understanding, could rites and music fail to flourish? Truly, those who act rashly without understanding are always prone to excess. Excess inevitably brings the faults of violence and disorder, and this is why rites and music fail to flourish.

Once the sage understands Heaven and Earth, he can give expression in his institutions to what he alone has apprehended in his heart. In accord with righteousness, he establishes what did not previously exist; following human feelings, he gives them measured and patterned expression. Everything by which he grades the noble and the humble and determines degrees of closeness and distance in kinship manifests the principle of differentiation. Through order he assists order, thereby aiding Heaven and Earth in bringing things to completion. How could he go so far as to create disorder through excessive regulation? He corrects the pitch standards to harmonize sounds and examines tones to establish music. Everything by which he reaches spirits and human beings and brings harmony to those above and below makes manifest the transforming power of union. Through harmony he strengthens harmony, thereby aiding Heaven and Earth in generating things. How could he go so far as to produce violence through excessive innovation? Music is created in accordance with Heaven; one must understand the harmony of Heaven and Earth…

…and only then can one create it. Ritual is fashioned in accordance with Earth: only after understanding the order of Heaven and Earth can one establish it. How could ritual and music be easy to discuss! Now, it is certainly true that ritual and music are rooted in Heaven and Earth and created by sages. The essential point, however, is that sages first possess virtue as their foundation. Thus, when they give it expression in institutions, these invariably accord with Heaven and Earth. This is what is meant by acting before Heaven without Heaven opposing them, and acting after Heaven in observance of its seasons. A Han scholar said: “Only the Son of Heaven establishes the supreme standard of centrality and harmony.” Surely this, too, is a statement that recognizes the foundation!

title: 嘉靖七年順天府鄉試錄
text:
考試官右庶子韓批近日論塲多剽竊舊文
補綴成篇欲學古者則又不式此作止就時格以
程子本旨鋪叙成章亦未嘗不竒可為塲屋文字
式矣
論曰聖王所以能勝天下之大任者亦惟有以
得天下之大法而操天下之大要而已矣夫天
下至大也成天下之治大治也聖王一身當天
下之大而欲以致天下之大治大任也負其大
也使不大其務而小焉以當之則心日益憂身
===
日益勞而天下日益不可理矣聖王於此有法
焉責之衆職而已矣有要焉求賢以任衆職而
已矣得其法而操其要然後天下之治成而聖
王者始為不負於天下而能勝天下之大矣程
子曰聖王能致天下之治要亦以其法與要而
言之也夫天下之事必有其法而法必有其要
事無其法則雜然無所從事而其事不可為法
無其要則貿然無所持循而其法不可行聖王
所以能致天下之治者無他法與要而已矣聖

論曰：聖王所以能勝天下之大任者，亦惟有以得天下之大法而操天下之大要而已矣。夫天下至大也，成天下之治，大治也。聖王一身當天下之大，而欲以致天下之大治，大任也。負其大也，使不大其務而小焉以當之，則心日益憂，身日益勞，而天下日益不可理矣。聖王於此有法焉，責之衆職而已矣；有要焉，求賢以任衆職而已矣。得其法而操其要，然後天下之治成，而聖王者始為不負於天下，而能勝天下之大矣。程子曰：「聖王能致天下之治。」要亦以其法與要而言之也。夫天下之事必有其法，而法必有其要。事無其法，則雜然無所從事，而其事不可為；法無其要，則貿然無所持循，而其法不可行。聖王所以能致天下之治者，無他，法與要而已矣。聖

This composition simply follows the contemporary form, developing Master Cheng’s original meaning into a coherent essay. Yet it is by no means without distinction and can serve as a model for examination writing.

The discourse reads: The reason sage kings can discharge the great responsibility of governing all under Heaven is simply that they possess its great governing method and grasp its essential principle. All under Heaven is vast indeed; bringing it into order is an achievement of great governance. For a sage king, in his single person, to shoulder responsibility for this vast realm and seek to bring it into great order is a great charge. Bearing so great a burden, if he fails to give his endeavors a corresponding breadth and instead approaches it in a petty way, his mind will grow more anxious each day, his body more weary, and the realm ever less governable. Here the sage king has a method: simply to assign responsibility to the various offices. He has an essential principle: simply to seek worthy men to fill those offices. Only after securing this method and grasping this essential principle can order be established throughout the realm. Only then does the sage king fulfill his obligation to all under Heaven and prove capable of bearing its vast burden. Master Cheng said, “Sage kings can bring order to all under Heaven.” His point, too, concerns their method and essential principle. The affairs of the realm must have a method, and that method must have an essential principle. Without a method, affairs become confused, leaving no basis for action, and cannot be accomplished. Without an essential principle, a method leaves one proceeding blindly, with nothing to hold to or follow, and cannot be put into practice. title: 嘉靖七年順天府鄉試錄
text:
王者負高天下之才神化變通無感不應其於
天下之事固宜伸縮運用取辨於指顧呼吸之
間亦何必仰于衆職之脩賢才之舉而後治邪
夫聖王之所以聖者正以其能駕馭天下之職
網羅一世之才以天下為度者也如此則天下
之才皆其才神化變通達之天下而聖人之才
於是始高於天下而天下之治無難致者矣聖
王之治亦大矣在朝廷吾見其庶績煕凝焉在
四方吾見其風動咸寧焉在四裔吾見其蠻夷
===
率服焉下至於庶類百工之小吾見其草木鳥
獸之生金皮木石之技亦咸若其性得其理焉
治若是其大也聖王豈事事而親之哉以天下
之職治天下之事耳使聖王於此苟徒恃乎一
人之聰明而欲以一人治之則聖王者固亦一
人之才耳而吾神化變通之妙將滯於無用安
能有以成天下之治哉是故責之衆職焉興事
考成而已矣懋官懋賞而已矣罔兼罔知而已
矣在朝廷有公卿大夫也責之以燮理崇廣之

王之治亦大矣在朝廷吾見其庶績熙凝焉在
四方吾見其風動咸寧焉在四裔吾見其蠻夷
===
率服焉下至於庶類百王之小吾見其草木鳥
獸之生金皮木石之技亦咸若其性得其理焉
治若是其大也聖王豈事事而親之哉以天下
之職治天下之事耳使聖王於此苟徒恃乎一
人之聰明而欲以一人治之則聖王者固亦一
人之才耳而吾神化變通之妙將滯於無用安
能有以成天下之治哉是故責之衆職焉興事
考成而已矣懋官懋賞而已矣罔無罔知而已
矣在朝廷有公卿大夫也責之以燮理崇廣之
punctuated:
王者負高天下之才，神化變通，無感不應。其於天下之事，固宜伸縮運用，取辨於指顧呼吸之間，亦何必仰于衆職之脩、賢才之舉而後治邪？夫聖王之所以聖者，正以其能駕馭天下之職，網羅一世之才，以天下為度者也。如此，則天下之才皆其才，神化變通，達之天下，而聖人之才於是始高於天下，而天下之治無難致者矣。
聖王之治亦大矣！在朝廷，吾見其庶績煕凝焉；在四方，吾見其風動咸寧焉；在四裔，吾見其蠻夷率服焉；下至於庶類百工之小，吾見其草木鳥獸之生、金皮木石之技，亦咸若其性，得其理焉。治若是其大也，聖王豈事事而親之哉？以天下之職治天下之事耳。使聖王於此苟徒恃乎一人之聰明，而欲以一人治之，則聖王者固亦一人之才耳，而吾神化變通之妙將滯於無用，安能有以成天下之治哉？是故責之衆職焉，興事考成而已矣，懋官懋賞而已矣，罔兼罔知而已矣。在朝廷有公卿大夫也，責之以燮理崇廣之
translation_en:
…the sage king possesses talents surpassing those of all under Heaven; his transformations are wondrous, his adaptations unfailing, and he responds to every stimulus. In handling the affairs of the realm, surely he should be able to adjust and deploy his abilities, settling matters with a gesture or glance, in the space of a breath. Why, then, must he depend upon the proper discharge of the various offices and the advancement of worthy talent before good government can be achieved? What makes the sage king a sage is precisely his ability to direct the offices of the realm, gather the talents of an entire age, and take all under Heaven as his measure. Thus the talents of the realm all become his talents, and his wondrous transformations and adaptations reach throughout the realm. Only then do the sage’s talents surpass those of all under Heaven, and bringing about good government presents no difficulty.
Vast indeed is the sage king’s governance! At court, I see all achievements flourishing and firmly established; throughout the land, I see his influence moving like the wind and bringing peace to all; in the four outer regions, I see the non-Chinese peoples all submitting. Descending even to the lesser matters of the many kinds of living things and the hundred crafts, I see that the growth of plants, trees, birds, and beasts, and the techniques of working metal, hide, wood, and stone, all accord with their respective natures and attain their proper principles. With governance so vast, how could the sage king personally attend to every affair? He simply uses the offices of the realm to manage its affairs. If, in these circumstances, the sage king relied solely on one person’s intelligence and sought to govern through that one person alone, then even he would possess only one person’s talents. The subtle power of his wondrous transformations and adaptations would become obstructed and useless. How could he thereby bring about good government throughout the realm? Thus he holds the various offices responsible: he need only initiate undertakings and assess their completion, confer offices and rewards for merit, and neither take on concurrent duties nor concern himself with every detail. At court there are the Three Dukes, the Nine Chamberlains, and grand masters; he charges them with the responsibility of harmonizing affairs and elevating and broadening …

title: 嘉靖七年順天府鄉試錄
text:
任在四方有州牧侯伯也責之以惠康屏翰之
任在四裔有尹帥師長也責之以脩攘懷柔之
任下至百司庶府山林川澤之吏亦皆使之隨
其職而各稱其任焉職若是其眾也聖王豈官
官而蒞之哉以天下之賢任天下之職耳夫賢
才之生傑出群類抱道自重非可常得亦非可
以苟得也使聖王於此搜羅之不以其道聘待
之不以其禮自謂天下之才皆出吾下苟可以
集吾事者皆可任之以官而吾之才自足以鼓
===
舞驅策使奔走於吾而莫敢後者奚必賢才而
後可哉如此則賢者止於千里之外而讒諂奸
諛之徒翩然雜進豈惟不足以成吾治彼將托
吾神化變通之權以售其蠹治之技者將無所
不至而聖王之治隳矣是故付之賢人焉籲俊
尊帝而已矣旁招俊乂而已矣從容德從義德
而已矣求之不可不廣也拔之於庶僚舉之於
側陋而不以其方待之不可無禮也將之以玉
帛申之以恭敬而曲盡其道任之不可不專也

集吾事者皆可任之以官而吾之才自足以鼓

帛申之以恭敬而盡其道焉之不可不尊道
punctuated: 任。在四方有州牧侯伯也，責之以惠康屏翰之任；在四裔有尹帥師長也，責之以脩攘懷柔之任。下至百司庶府山林川澤之吏，亦皆使之隨其職而各稱其任焉。職若是其眾也，聖王豈官官而蒞之哉？以天下之賢任天下之職耳。夫賢才之生，傑出群類，抱道自重，非可常得，亦非可以苟得也。使聖王於此搜羅之不以其道，聘待之不以其禮，自謂天下之才皆出吾下，苟可以集吾事者，皆可任之以官，而吾之才自足以鼓舞驅策，使奔走於吾而莫敢後者，奚必賢才而後可哉？如此，則賢者止於千里之外，而讒諂奸諛之徒翩然雜進。豈惟不足以成吾治？彼將托吾神化變通之權，以售其蠹治之技者，將無所不至，而聖王之治隳矣。是故付之賢人焉，籲俊尊帝而已矣，旁招俊乂而已矣，從容德、從義德而已矣。求之不可不廣也，拔之於庶僚，舉之於側陋，而不以其方；待之不可無禮也，將之以玉帛，申之以恭敬，而曲盡其道；任之不可不專也。
translation_en:
…duties. Throughout the regions there are regional governors, marquises, and earls, charged with bringing the people well-being and peace and serving as protective bulwarks. On the outer frontiers there are administrators, commanders, and military chiefs, charged with maintaining defenses, repelling incursions, and winning allegiance through conciliation. Down to the officials of the various offices and bureaus, and those responsible for mountains, forests, rivers, and marshes, all are likewise made to discharge their respective functions and fulfill their responsibilities. With offices so numerous, could the sage king personally oversee each one? He simply appoints the worthy men of the realm to its offices.

Worthy and talented men stand out from their fellows, hold fast to the Way, and respect their own worth. They cannot always be found, nor can they be obtained by careless means. Suppose the sage king sought them without following the proper way and invited and received them without the proper rites, saying to himself: “All the talent in the realm falls below mine. Anyone who can accomplish my business may be appointed to office. My own abilities suffice to inspire and direct them, making them hurry to serve me, none daring to lag behind. Why must I have worthy and talented men before anything can be done?” In that case, the worthy would remain a thousand li away, while slanderers, flatterers, schemers, and sycophants would come flocking into office. Would this merely fail to bring about good government? Relying on my authority to effect wondrous transformations and adapt to changing circumstances, they would go to every length to practice their arts of corrupting government, and the sage king’s governance would fall into ruin.

Thus he entrusts these responsibilities to worthy men: simply calling upon outstanding men to honor the Supreme Sovereign, recruiting outstanding and capable men far and wide, and following men of tolerant virtue and men of righteous virtue. The search for them must be broad: he promotes them from among subordinate officials and raises them from humble obscurity, without regard to their place of origin. They must be received with ritual propriety: he presents jade and silk and reinforces these gifts with reverence and respect, fulfilling every detail of the proper way. They must be entrusted with undivided responsibility…

title: 嘉靖七年順天府鄉試錄
text:
去讒遠色賤貨貴德而務竭其誠如是而賢者
不起帝臣之願王賓之思者未之有也夫然後
因其才器之高下而為職任之大小孰能論道
弘化熈載浚明則使之為公卿為大夫孰能牧
民馭衆蕃王亮采則使之為州牧為侯伯孰能
連衆發謀折衝禦侮則使之為尹帥為師長以
至一才一藝之士苟可以司一職舉一事者亦
皆使之以為內外百司庶府之官焉才無不用
也用無不當也官無非才也由是聖王者雖不
===
必身任天下之事而天下之治皆其治也三事
脩六官舉百司飭而庶政熈寧矣教化行衣食
足暴亂息而風動咸寧矣武烈揚軍威振國勢
張而蠻夷率服矣陰陽和風雨時寒暑節而萬
物咸若矣下至百工之微亦莫不各精其能信
其度而各得其理矣聖王者於是乎有以盡大
君之責而勝天下之任焉此無他得其法而操
其要耳抑論之人主勞于求賢而逸于任人如
天運于上日月四時各司其職而天無所預焉

不起帝臣之願王賓之思者未之有也夫然後

也用無不當也官無非才也由是聖王者雖不

其要耳抑論之人主勞于求賢而逸于任人如

punctuated: 去讒遠色，賤貨貴德，而務竭其誠。如是而賢者不起帝臣之願、王賓之思者，未之有也。夫然後，因其才器之高下而為職任之大小。孰能論道弘化、熈載浚明，則使之為公卿、為大夫；孰能牧民馭衆、蕃王亮采，則使之為州牧、為侯伯；孰能連衆發謀、折衝禦侮，則使之為尹帥、為師長。以至一才一藝之士，苟可以司一職、舉一事者，亦皆使之以為內外百司庶府之官焉。才無不用也，用無不當也，官無非才也。由是聖王者，雖不必身任天下之事，而天下之治皆其治也。三事脩，六官舉，百司飭，而庶政熈寧矣；教化行，衣食足，暴亂息，而風動咸寧矣；武烈揚，軍威振，國勢張，而蠻夷率服矣；陰陽和，風雨時，寒暑節，而萬物咸若矣。下至百工之微，亦莫不各精其能、信其度，而各得其理矣。聖王者於是乎有以盡大君之責，而勝天下之任焉。此無他，得其法而操其要耳。抑論之，人主勞于求賢，而逸于任人，如天運于上，日月四時各司其職，而天無所預焉。
translation_en:
…dismiss slanderers, keep sensual attractions at a distance, hold wealth cheap and virtue dear, and strive to show the utmost sincerity. When this is done, no worthy person could fail to wish to become the emperor’s minister or to aspire to be the king’s honored guest. Only then should the scope of their offices and responsibilities be determined according to the degree of their ability and capacity. Those capable of expounding the Way, extending moral transformation, making undertakings prosper, and illuminating virtue should be appointed dukes, ministers, and grand masters. Those capable of shepherding the people, governing the multitude, protecting the king, and assisting in affairs should be appointed regional governors and feudal lords. Those capable of rallying the multitude, devising plans, repelling aggression, and resisting insult should be appointed governors and commanders, military leaders and chiefs. Even men possessing only one talent or skill, provided they can discharge one office or accomplish one task, should all be appointed officials in the various agencies and offices at court and in the provinces. No talent would go unused; no appointment would be inappropriate; no office would lack a capable occupant.

Thus, although the sage king need not personally undertake the affairs of the realm, all the realm’s good government would be his achievement. The Three Dukes would discharge their duties, the six ministries would perform their functions, and the hundred offices would be kept in order, bringing prosperity and tranquility to every branch of government. Moral instruction would spread, clothing and food would suffice, and violence and disorder would cease; all would respond to his influence as to the wind and enjoy peace. Martial achievements would be celebrated, military might would be manifest, and the power of the state would expand, so that all the non-Chinese peoples would submit. Yin and yang would be harmonious, wind and rain timely, and cold and heat seasonable, so that all things would flourish in due order. Even the humblest artisans would each perfect their skills, faithfully observe their standards, and attain the proper principles of their craft. The sage king would thereby fulfill the responsibilities of a great ruler and prove equal to the charge of governing the realm. This would come from nothing other than finding the right method and grasping its essentials.

To consider the matter further: the ruler labors in seeking worthy men but enjoys ease in employing them. He is like Heaven moving above: the sun, moon, and four seasons each perform their functions, while Heaven itself need not intervene.…

於大廷之上深宮之中兢兢業業未嘗少替總
攬紀綱之外則精一執中之務也苟恃乎賢人
在位乃逸樂怠荒置朝政講勸于不聞曰吾有
賢人可任也則其亂亡之至亦不旋踵矣故伊
尹曰自周有終相亦惟終嗣王罔克有終相亦
罔終然則人主者固不可侵臣下之職亦不可
失人主之柄謹論

translation_en:
Nevertheless, the emperors and kings of antiquity were indeed single-minded in entrusting responsibilities to worthy men and did not encroach upon the duties of subordinate officials. Yet in the great court and within the secluded palace, they remained vigilant and conscientious, never relaxing their efforts in the slightest. Beyond maintaining overall command of the governing order, their task was to remain discerning and single-minded and to hold fast to the Mean. If, relying on worthy men being in office, a ruler indulges in pleasure, becomes idle and negligent, and turns a deaf ear to court affairs and to instruction and admonition, saying, “I have worthy men whom I can employ,” disorder and ruin will follow before he can turn on his heel. Thus Yi Yin said: “If he himself is thorough and carries matters through to the end [?], his ministers too will carry them through; if the succeeding king cannot carry matters through to the end, his ministers too will fail to do so.” Thus a ruler must neither encroach upon his subjects’ duties nor relinquish the authority belonging to the ruler. Respectfully submitted as a discourse.

Memorial

text:
賜宴秘書省者臣等誠懽誠忭稽首頓首謹
言
講幄
天開式稽古以資治儒林地切用大烹以養
賢肆周室之崇文光生簡册曁漢廷之設
醴榮感章縫自昔已然於今爲盛茲蓋伏
遇
聰明天授
===
===

慶肇龍潛

…having been granted a banquet at the Palace Library. We, your servants, sincerely rejoice and exult; we bow our heads to the ground and kowtow, and respectfully submit:
The imperial lecture pavilion opens beneath Heaven, where antiquity is examined to aid governance; the community of scholars stands close to the throne, where sumptuous offerings nourish the worthy. Thus the Zhou royal house’s reverence for culture brought radiance to its written records, and the Han court’s provision of sweet wine moved its scholars with the honor bestowed upon them. So it has been since antiquity; today it flourishes still more greatly. This is because we have humbly encountered Your Majesty, endowed by Heaven with intelligence, possessed of heroic martial prowess and divine plans. Auspicious blessings began while the dragon still lay hidden; brilliant cultural accomplishment shone forth in the tiger’s transformation.
Your imperial heart shuns ease, and accordingly you have drawn up a plan for revering Heaven. Your sagely filial devotion grows ever greater, and you scrupulously observe the rites of inquiring after your parents’ well-being. There is no great guiding principle or law of the former kings that you do not study and investigate; the excellent plans and counsels of more recent times have likewise received your scrutiny. Taking what is good from others, you have found yourself a teacher. Now that the readings have concluded, we have undeservedly enjoyed the fare of the imperial kitchen. In the Orchid Terrace and the book-filled pavilions, officials in ceremonial dress gather in the glory of the two drafting offices; fine wines and exquisite dishes arrive in succession, offering the delights of the Eight Delicacies. Your kindness moistens us like heavy dew; your bounty pours forth like the clouds of the hexagram Waiting. Lectures in the Chongzheng Hall continue the splendid precedents of former reigns; the banquet bestowed at Yujin lets us savor the lingering fragrance of recent days.

We, your servants, have long unworthily occupied the ranks of distinguished officials and are deeply ashamed to have eaten without earning our keep. Though we have eaten our fill of the ancients’ dregs, how could we call these the rich nourishment of the Way? Drinking the mellow harmony of your supreme virtue, we have become intoxicated at heart without knowing it. How could we fail to observe the rules bequeathed by the former teacher, walking when he walks and hastening when he hastens; or to expend the humble loyalty of our limited learning, eating our sovereign’s food and performing our sovereign’s work?

We humbly pray that you relax the prohibition on Learning of the Way, so as to employ true Confucians; and establish plans for restoration, so as to exalt the Central Realm. May the fortunes of letters forever accord with the fortunes of the state, extending the blessings of your dynastic succession for ten thousand years. May your servants’ hearts truly accord with the sovereign’s heart, united in virtue amid the flourishing partnership of an enlightened ruler and worthy ministers. Comment by Associate Examiner Li, Instructor: “Revering Heaven, loving the people, and emulating the ancestors are practices that His Majesty personally carries out today. title: 嘉靖七年順天府鄉試錄
text:
考試官右庶子韓批畏
天法
祖得民
聖政之大無以過此子能言之必佳士也
人君莫大乎合天人之心莫要乎法祖宗
之道盖天之所助者順也必思順而天心
格人之所助者信也必履信而人心孚人
君之德誠莫有大於此矣然祖宗之心即
天人之心祖宗之道即信順之道苟能法
===
之則天人其有不合者哉請敬陳之履信
思順者孔子之言也躬信順以先天下蘇
軾之告其君也順以得天心信以收人心
真德秀之告其君也惜乎當時之君舉不
足以語此而惟我
太祖高皇帝以天與人歸之主妙體信達順之
化真能行乎二臣之說矣嘗伏讀
聖諭有曰天道微妙難知人事感通易見君能
脩德則七政順度雨暘應期災害不生矣

punctuated:
考試官右庶子韓批：畏天、法祖、得民，聖政之大無以過此。子能言之，必佳士也。

人君莫大乎合天人之心，莫要乎法祖宗之道。盖天之所助者順也，必思順而天心格；人之所助者信也，必履信而人心孚。人君之德，誠莫有大於此矣。然祖宗之心即天人之心，祖宗之道即信順之道。苟能法之，則天人其有不合者哉？請敬陳之。履信思順者，孔子之言也；躬信順以先天下，蘇軾之告其君也；順以得天心，信以收人心，真德秀之告其君也。惜乎當時之君，舉不足以語此，而惟我太祖高皇帝，以天與人歸之主，妙體信達順之化，真能行乎二臣之說矣。嘗伏讀聖諭，有曰：「天道微妙難知，人事感通易見。君能脩德，則七政順度，雨暘應期，災害不生矣。」
translation_en:
Comment by Examiner Han, Right Mentor: “Revere Heaven, emulate the ancestors, and win the people: nothing in sagely government surpasses these great principles. Since you can articulate them, you must be a worthy scholar.”

For a ruler, nothing is greater than bringing himself into accord with the hearts of Heaven and the people; nothing is more essential than emulating the Way of his ancestors. What Heaven assists is compliance: he must therefore contemplate compliance, and Heaven’s heart will be moved. What people assist is trustworthiness: he must therefore act with trustworthiness, and the people’s hearts will have confidence in him. Truly, no virtue of a ruler is greater than this. Yet the hearts of the ancestors are precisely the hearts of Heaven and the people, and the Way of the ancestors is precisely the Way of trustworthiness and compliance. If he can emulate them, how could he fail to accord with Heaven and the people? Allow me respectfully to explain.

“Act with trustworthiness and contemplate compliance” was Confucius’s teaching. “Personally embody trustworthiness and compliance to lead all under Heaven” was Su Shi’s admonition to his ruler. “Through compliance, win Heaven’s heart; through trustworthiness, gather the people’s hearts” was Zhen Dexiu’s admonition to his ruler. Regrettably, the rulers of their times were all unworthy of being addressed on these matters. Only our Emperor Taizu Gao, as a sovereign whom Heaven supported and to whom the people gave their allegiance, wondrously embodied the transforming power of trustworthiness and thorough compliance, and truly put into practice the teachings of these two ministers.

I once reverently read an imperial admonition that stated: “The Way of Heaven is subtle and difficult to know; the influence of human affairs upon it and its response are readily apparent. If the ruler can cultivate virtue, the seven celestial luminaries will follow their proper courses, rain and sunshine will arrive at their appointed times, and calamities will not arise.”

title: 嘉靖七年順天府鄉試錄

也又曰得天下者得民心也恤其老則天
下之爲子弟者悅恤其幼則天下之爲父
兄者悅其心有不歸者寡矣盖恤老幼以
孚民心而民應之此所以爲信也是皆行
之已驗於當時而後言之以示於後世也
恭惟
皇上稟神聖之資進誠明之學其事天也郊禋
之禮務極精誠念慮之微恒存戒愼宜無

For by cultivating virtue one accords with Heaven’s heart, and Heaven responds: this is what constitutes accord. He also said: “To gain All-under-Heaven is to gain the people’s hearts. Care for their elders, and all those under Heaven who are sons and younger brothers will rejoice; care for their young, and all those under Heaven who are fathers and elder brothers will rejoice. text:
養民而勿事乎虛文凡安老懷幼之政本
之以真心施之以實惠也由是順足以得
天心妙契於感假之際而眷顧之有加信
足以收人心潜孚於神化之餘而會歸之
無外轉乖氣而為和氣易咎徵而為休徵
政教洽而禮樂興天地位而萬物育豈非
信順之極功哉抑聞人君之德有三敬天
也愛民也法祖也然民即天也故君以民
為天祖亦天也故聖人以祖配天書云天
===
聰明自我民聰明天明畏自我民明威釋
之者曰天人一理通達無間民心所存即
天理所在也詩云畏天之威于時保之釋
之者曰畏天所以畏文王也天與文王一
也盖可見矣後世大臣乃謂天變不足畏
人言不足恤祖宗不足法者豈非萬世之
罪人哉區區芹曝之忠願轉達之
聖聰焉幸甚
第二問
alt_text:
養民而勿事乎虛文凡安老懷幼之政本
之以真心施之以實惠也由是順足以得
天心妙契於感假之際而眷顧之有加信
足以收人心潛孚於神化之餘而會歸之
無外轉乖氣而為和氣易咎徵而為休徵
政教洽而禮樂興天地位而萬物育豈非
信順之極功哉抑聞人君之德有三敬天
也愛民也法祖也然民即天也故君以民
為天祖亦天也故聖人以祖配天書云天
===
聰明自我民聰明天明畏自我民明威釋
之者曰天人一理通達無間民心所存即
天理所在也詩云畏天之威于時保之釋
之者曰畏天所以畏文王也天與文王一
也盖可見矣後世大臣乃謂天變不足畏

罪人哉區區芹曝之忠願轉達之
聖聽焉幸甚
第二問
punctuated:
養民而勿事乎虛文，凡安老懷幼之政，本之以真心，施之以實惠也。由是，順足以得天心，妙契於感假之際，而眷顧之有加；信足以收人心，潜孚於神化之餘，而會歸之無外。轉乖氣而為和氣，易咎徵而為休徵，政教洽而禮樂興，天地位而萬物育，豈非信順之極功哉？抑聞人君之德有三：敬天也，愛民也，法祖也。然民即天也，故君以民為天；祖亦天也，故聖人以祖配天。《書》云：「天聰明自我民聰明，天明畏自我民明威。」釋之者曰：「天人一理，通達無間，民心所存，即天理所在也。」《詩》云：「畏天之威，于時保之。」釋之者曰：「畏天所以畏文王也，天與文王一也。」盖可見矣。後世大臣乃謂天變不足畏、人言不足恤、祖宗不足法者，豈非萬世之罪人哉？區區芹曝之忠，願轉達之聖聰焉，幸甚！

第二問
translation_en:
…nourish the people without attending merely to empty formalities. Every measure to bring peace to the elderly and care to the young should be rooted in a sincere heart and implemented through tangible benefits. In this way, accordance will suffice to win Heaven’s favor, achieving a wondrous concord as sincerity reaches Heaven and calls forth its response, so that its gracious regard increases. Trustworthiness will suffice to win the people’s hearts, silently gaining their confidence through the effects of spiritual transformation, so that all turn toward the ruler, none remaining outside. Discordant influences will become harmonious ones, and ominous portents will become auspicious signs. Government and moral instruction will reach everywhere, rites and music will flourish, Heaven and Earth will occupy their proper places, and the myriad things will be nurtured. Would this not be the highest achievement of trustworthiness and accordance?

I have also heard that a ruler has three virtues: revering Heaven, loving the people, and emulating his ancestors. Yet the people are Heaven; thus the ruler takes the people as his Heaven. The ancestors, too, are Heaven; thus the sage associates his ancestor with Heaven in sacrifice. The Book of Documents says: “Heaven’s hearing and sight come from the hearing and sight of our people; Heaven’s manifest awe comes from the manifest authority of our people.” Its commentator says: “Heaven and humanity share one principle, communicating without any separation. Where the people’s hearts abide is precisely where Heaven’s principle resides.” The Book of Odes says: “Fear Heaven’s majesty, and thereby preserve it.” Its commentator says: “To fear Heaven is to fear King Wen. Heaven and King Wen are one.” This makes the matter clear. Yet a great minister of a later age declared that changes in Heaven need not be feared, people’s words need not be heeded, and the ancestors need not be emulated. Was he not a sinner for all ages?

My humble loyalty is like the offering of celery or the warmth of the sun. I would count myself most fortunate if these words could be conveyed to His Majesty’s hearing.

Second Policy Question

孟紱

同考試官訓導張批：理數之精，易範備矣。性資高邁者，可與共學。子能融會八卦九章體變奇偶表裡經緯之妙，而一主於理，亦嘗究心於此也夫！宜錄之，以式後學。

同考試官教諭李批：理數一策，正欲觀士子身心之學。它卷率多枝詞臆說，牽强可厭。獨此作考究精詳，一本之理，以定乎數，盖積學有待之士也。輸服！輸服！

同考試官主事方批：理寓乎數，數不外乎理。自詞藝之工，數學之難明久矣。吾子素究心於彰往知来之奥者，肆有是答。

考試官右庶子方批：士子惟攻史學，不攻數學，故他策類能鋪敘，至此問則窘矣。擇精而語詳者，僅見此篇。

考試官右庶子韓批：易範用異而理同，及宋儒著述之得失，一能言之。宜錄以式。

對：數之為用有不同，而聖賢之著述亦不
translation_en:
Meng Fu 孟紱

Comment by Associate Examiner Zhang, Assistant Instructor: The essentials of principle and number are fully contained in the Book of Changes and the Great Plan. Those of lofty natural endowment are worthy companions in learning. You have comprehensively grasped the subtleties of the eight trigrams and nine sections—their configurations and transformations, odd and even numbers, outward and inward aspects, and interwoven relationships—while consistently taking principle as your guide. You must indeed have devoted thought to this subject! This answer should be recorded as a model for later students.

Comment by Associate Examiner Li, Instructor: This policy question on principle and number was intended precisely to reveal candidates’ learning in the cultivation of body and mind. Most other papers abound in extraneous language and conjecture, strained and tiresome. This composition alone investigates the subject with precision and thoroughness, grounding itself entirely in principle to establish the workings of number. Its author is surely a scholar who has accumulated learning while awaiting his opportunity. I yield in admiration! I yield in admiration!

Comment by Associate Examiner Fang, Secretary: Principle resides in number, and number does not lie outside principle. Since literary craftsmanship became refined [?], the learning of numbers has long been difficult to elucidate. You have habitually devoted yourself to the mysteries of making the past manifest and knowing what is to come; hence this answer.

Comment by Examiner Fang, Right Vice Supervisor of Instruction: Candidates devote themselves solely to historical learning, neglecting the learning of numbers. Thus, although they can generally develop their responses to the other policy questions at length, they find themselves at a loss when they reach this one. This is the only essay I have seen that selects the essential points and discusses them in detail.

Comment by Examiner Han, Right Vice Supervisor of Instruction: The Book of Changes and the Great Plan differ in application but share the same principle. This answer can explain all of this, together with the merits and shortcomings of the writings of Song Confucian scholars. It should be recorded as a model.

In reply: Numbers have differing applications, and the writings of sages and worthies likewise are not…

title: 嘉靖七年順天府鄉試錄
text:
同其理則一而已矣理之一則不害其用
之不同著述之不同也聖賢之著述豈聖
賢自爲一端臆想之說哉數有是理也聖
賢爲之著述以發其蘊耳聖賢何以知之
也揆之理而已矣聖賢之著述一於理也
學者論聖賢之著述也亦一於理而已矣
請因明問而答之道原于一而散於萬原
者理也散者數也天下有不同之數而無
不同之理理者數之神宰也數者理之形
===
象也非理則數不生非數則理不著舍數
而言理者虛無之學也舍理而言數者技
術之流也故吾道者合理與數而言之也
昔者伏羲氏繼天而王龍馬負圖出於河
所謂一六居北二七居南三八居東四九
居西五十居中者是也卦之理寓焉伏羲
因而則之以爲乾兌離震巽坎艮坤之八
卦六十四卦既成文王繫卦辭周公繫爻
辭筮則用之一耳大禹治水成功神龜負

…differ, yet their underlying principle is one and nothing more. The unity of principle does not preclude differences in its applications or in the writings that expound it. Could the writings of the sages and worthies be fanciful theories they devised on their own? Numbers possess this principle, and the sages and worthies wrote simply to reveal what lay within them. How did they know it? Simply by examining things against principle. The writings of the sages and worthies are united in principle; scholars discussing those writings must likewise take principle as their sole standard.

Allow me to answer your illuminating question accordingly. The Way originates in unity and disperses into the myriad things. At its source is principle; in its dispersed manifestations are numbers. In all under Heaven, numbers differ, but principle does not. Principle is the spiritual governor of numbers; numbers are the visible forms of principle. Without principle, numbers do not arise; without numbers, principle does not become manifest. To abandon numbers and speak of principle is the learning of emptiness and nothingness; to abandon principle and speak of numbers is the pursuit of mere techniques. Thus, those who follow our Way discuss principle and numbers together.

Long ago, when Fuxi succeeded Heaven as king, a dragon-horse emerged from the Yellow River bearing a diagram. This is the arrangement in which one and six occupy the north, two and seven the south, three and eight the east, four and nine the west, and five and ten the center. The principle of the trigrams was lodged within it. Fuxi accordingly took it as his pattern and made the eight trigrams: Qian, Dui, Li, Zhen, Xun, Kan, Gen, and Kun. Once the sixty-four hexagrams had been formed, King Wen appended the hexagram statements, and the Duke of Zhou appended the line statements. 書出於洛所謂戴九履一左三右七二四
爲肩六八爲足者是也範之理寓焉禹因
而陳之以爲五行五事八政五紀皇極三
德稽疑庶徵福極之九疇九疇旣列箕子
衍其義武王傳其學筮則目之一耳易筮
起於前古至朱子作啓蒙以盡乎蓍之變
其揲也以四三變而一爻具九變而小成

…a writing emerged from the Luo River. This is what is described as “nine above and one below, three on the left and seven on the right, two and four as the shoulders, and six and eight as the feet.” The principles of the Great Plan were lodged within it. Yu accordingly set them forth as the nine categories: the Five Elements, the Five Personal Conducts, the Eight Affairs of Government, the Five Regulators of Time, the August Ultimate, the Three Virtues, the Resolution of Doubts, the Various Signs, and Blessings and Calamities. Once the nine categories had been arrayed, Jizi elaborated their meaning, and King Wu transmitted their teaching; stalk divination was merely one item within it.
Divination through the Changes originated in remote antiquity. In time Master Zhu wrote the Introduction to the Study of the Changes (Qimeng), fully exploring the transformations of the milfoil stalks. The stalks are counted off in groups of four; three transformations complete one line, and nine transformations produce the lesser completion, a trigram. Qian is one, Dui two, Li three, Zhen four, Xun five, Kan six, Gen seven, and Kun eight. In general, once the trigrams reach eight, the secrets of the River Chart have already been disclosed. Proceeding from this, eighteen transformations produce the greater completion, a hexagram. Extending these by analogy, the transformations of the sixty-four hexagrams yield the full set of 4,096 hexagrams. Through them, the doubts of all under Heaven are resolved, and the undertakings of all under Heaven are settled.
For divination through the Great Plan, there was previously nothing that could be consulted. In time Master Cai wrote the August Ultimate (Huangji), elucidating the use of the milfoil stalks. The stalks are counted off in groups of three; one counting establishes the main division, and a second completes the subdivisions. One-one makes one; one-two makes two; one-three makes three; two-one makes four; two-two makes five; two-three makes six; three-one makes seven; three-two makes eight; and three-three makes nine. In general, once the numbers reach nine, the secrets of the Luo Writing have already been disclosed. Four countings complete eighty-one sections. title: 嘉靖七年順天府鄉試錄
text:
四會六千五百六十一數於是乎備天命
人事由是較焉吉凶禍福由是彰焉易之
揲四而其變三體方而用員也範之揲三
而其變二體員而用方也此執事所謂分
掛揲歸之法通變極數之妙考占成業之
義無一不同者盖理之同也於此不同則
亦不足以為數矣夫易廣矣大矣而範之
數直與之同流執事疑非蔡子之作愚生
亦謂數學自易以後雖代有作者經世放
===
於易而為之者也太玄潛虛之類支離破
碎强合難通未有如範數之大不用乎易
而能準乎易者此必上世以来有所秘傳
混於丹竈之家而蔡子得之於異人之授
不然則蔡子既聖矣乎何以能作也孔子
曰動則觀其變而玩其占乾之群龍用九
坤之永貞用六今朱子啓蒙考占之法四
爻五爻之變乃占之卦不變之爻易之爻
非九則六而不變之爻非七則八也易無

掛揲歸之法通變極數之妙考占成業之
義無一不同者盖理之同也於此不同則
亦不足以爲數矣夫易廣矣大矣而範之
數直與之同流執事疑非蔡子之作愚生
亦謂數學自易以後雖代有作者經世放
===
於易而爲之者也太玄潛虚之類支離破
碎强合難通未有如範數之大不用乎易
而能準乎易者此必上世以来有所秘傳
混於丹竈之家而蔡子得之於異人之授
不然則蔡子既聖矣乎何以能作也孔子
曰動則觀其變而玩其占乾之群龍用九
坤之永貞用六今朱子啓蒙考占之法四
爻五爻之變乃占之卦不變之爻易之爻
非九則六而不變之爻非七則八也易無
punctuated:
四會六千五百六十一數，於是乎備。天命人事由是較焉，吉凶禍福由是彰焉。易之揲四而其變三，體方而用員也；範之揲三而其變二，體員而用方也。此執事所謂分掛揲歸之法、通變極數之妙、考占成業之義，無一不同者，盖理之同也。於此不同，則亦不足以為數矣。夫易廣矣，大矣，而範之數直與之同流。執事疑非蔡子之作，愚生亦謂數學自易以後，雖代有作者，經世放於易而為之者也；太玄、潛虛之類，支離破碎，强合難通。未有如範數之大，不用乎易而能準乎易者。此必上世以来有所秘傳，混於丹竈之家，而蔡子得之於異人之授。不然，則蔡子既聖矣乎？何以能作也？

…the four combinations, comprising 6,561 numbers, are thus complete. Heaven’s mandate and human affairs are thereby made clear, and good and ill fortune, calamity and blessing, are thereby revealed. In the Changes, the stalks are counted off in fours, with three transformations: its substance is square, and its operation round. In the Great Plan, the stalks are counted off in threes, with two transformations: its substance is round, and its operation square. These are what you, sir, describe as the methods of dividing the stalks, setting one aside, counting them off, and gathering the remainders; the subtle art of comprehending transformations and exhausting numerical possibilities; and the significance of examining prognostications and bringing undertakings to completion. That they agree in every respect is because their underlying principle is the same. If they differed in this respect, they would not suffice as systems of numbers.
The Changes is broad and great, yet the numerical system of the Great Plan stands directly alongside it. You, sir, doubt that it was Master Cai’s creation. I, your humble student, likewise hold that, although every age since the Changes has produced writers on numerical learning, Ordering the World (Jingshi) was composed in imitation of the Changes. Works such as the Supreme Mystery (Taixuan) and Fathoming the Void (Qianxu) are disjointed and fragmentary; their forced correspondences are difficult to reconcile. None possesses the greatness of the Great Plan’s numerical system, which does not rely on the Changes yet can match it. This must have been secretly transmitted from high antiquity, surviving among practitioners of alchemy, until Master Cai received it through the instruction of an extraordinary person. Otherwise, must Master Cai already have been a sage? How else could he have devised it?

text:
七八之爻何自而占乎且於孔子觀變之
說有不合矣意者義理則先儒之論精詳
至到無可言者至於名物度數雖聖人亦
有未及學而或不盡者也夫天下古今理
而已矣理之同也遵之不以為阿理未同
也議之不以為僭此末學之臆見或亦執
事發問之意也大哉數乎天非數不覆地
非數不載人非數不成彰往知來者數也
通幽達變者數也藏神顯化者數也數豈
===
易言哉今執事問及愚生則不敢默也然
未知其是否謹對
第三問
馬一龍
同考試官訓導何批兵事尚變此篇以兵
法合與不合之中又証以兵法非有見於兵者
不能且惓惓以時弊之切者陳於篇終宏博之
才長遠之慮子盖有之矣擢之以魁多士豈不
宜哉

七八之爻，何自而占乎？且於孔子觀變之說有不合矣。意者，義理則先儒之論精詳至到，無可言者；至於名物度數，雖聖人亦有未及學而或不盡者也。夫天下古今，理而已矣。理之同也，遵之不以為阿；理未同也，議之不以為僭。此末學之臆見，或亦執事發問之意也。大哉，數乎！天非數不覆，地非數不載，人非數不成。彰往知來者，數也；通幽達變者，數也；藏神顯化者，數也。數豈易言哉！今執事問及愚生，則不敢默也，然未知其是否。謹對。

馬一龍

translation_en:
…lines numbered seven or eight: on what basis, then, can one divine from them? Moreover, this does not accord with Confucius’s teaching about observing changes. Perhaps, regarding moral principles, the discussions of earlier scholars are so penetrating, detailed, and thorough that nothing remains to be said; but regarding names and objects, measures and numbers, even sages may have things they have not yet studied and thus may not comprehend fully. Throughout the world, past and present, there is only principle. Where their understanding of principle agrees with ours, we follow it without considering this flattery; where it does not, we discuss it without considering this presumption. This is the conjecture of an unseasoned student, and perhaps it is also what you intended in posing your question. How great are numbers! Without numbers, Heaven could not cover all things, Earth could not bear them, and human beings could not attain fulfillment. Numbers illuminate the past and disclose the future; numbers penetrate the obscure and comprehend change; numbers harbor the numinous and manifest transformation. How could numbers be easy to discuss! Now that you have put this question to your unworthy student, I dare not remain silent, though I do not know whether my answer is correct. Respectfully submitted.
Third Policy Question
Ma Yilong

title: 嘉靖七年順天府鄉試錄
text:
同考試官助教薛批論兵一策諸士類能
掇拾成篇求之識權達變者盖鮮是作於昔人
攻守事踪條敷無遺且以知變不知變評隲之
卓有遠識篇末因循不振之慮切中時弊其亦
達權變之士歟異日柄用當不負茲喬選
考試官右庶子方批此策讀之終篇於吾有
感焉遂錄之
考試官右庶子韓批是嘗留心於兵法而志
欲見於推行者故錄
===
對有用兵之常有用兵之變常者固兵法
也變者亦兵法也自其常而觀之合乎兵
法者知兵法者也不合乎兵法者不知兵
法者也自其變而觀之合乎兵法者固知
兵法者也不合乎兵法者亦知兵法者也
夫兵者隨機應變因敵制勝者也何常形
之有哉昔趙括能讀父書奢不能難岳飛
好野戰不用古法盖飛知變而括不知變
也觀乎此則可以答明問矣夫威天下在

This essay systematically sets out the deeds of earlier men in attack and defense, leaving nothing out, and assesses them according to whether they understood how to adapt. Reply: There are constant principles in employing troops, and there are adaptations to changing circumstances. The constant principles are certainly military methods, but adaptations are military methods as well. Viewed in terms of constant principles, those who conform to military methods understand them, while those who do not conform do not understand them. Viewed in terms of adaptation, those who conform to military methods certainly understand them, but those who do not conform may also understand them. title: 嘉靖七年順天府鄉試錄
text:
於兵而主兵者在於將三軍之衆百萬之
師張設輕重在於一人為將者固不可以
不知兵用兵之妙存乎一心微乎微乎應
形於無窮而談兵者又不可不知變也崤
澠誠不可由也亞夫於是竟走藍田所謂
途有所不由者而馬援之困敗盖不知壺
頭之不可由矣華費誠不可攻也曹公所
以深入徐州所謂城有所不攻者而沈攸
之之走死盖不知郢郡之不可攻矣越王
===
許吳王之成范蠡不從其命乃叱公孫權
之請而遂成覇越之功董卓挾漢帝之命
皇甫嵩欲負其召乃忽梁衍之謀而竟就
匹夫之諒將在外君命有所不受蠡則知
之而嵩不知也吳起親裹贏糧與士卒分
勞苦守河西而拒强秦之兵宋義置酒大
會不恤士卒之凍餒留安陽而致項羽之
誅愛士卒當如愛子起則知之而義不知
也數將者其於兵法合之則成違之則敗

translation_en:
…upon military force, while command of military force rests with the general. The deployment and relative strength of the three armies, a host of a million men, depend upon a single person. A general certainly cannot afford to be ignorant of warfare. The subtle mastery of employing troops resides in the mind alone. How subtle! How subtle! It responds without limit to changing configurations; thus those who discuss warfare must also understand adaptation.

The Xiao–Mian route was indeed one not to take, and Yafu therefore ultimately went by way of Lantian. This exemplifies the saying, “There are roads one does not take.” Ma Yuan’s entrapment and defeat, however, arose from his failure to recognize that the route through Hutou was impassable. Hua and Fei were indeed places not to attack, which is why Lord Cao advanced deep into Xuzhou. This exemplifies the saying, “There are cities one does not attack.” Shen Youzhi’s flight and death, however, arose from his failure to recognize that Ying Commandery was not to be attacked.

The king of Yue consented to the king of Wu’s request for peace. Fan Li disobeyed his command, rebuked Gongsun Quan’s plea, and thereby accomplished the achievement of making Yue hegemon. Dong Zhuo invoked the authority of the Han emperor’s command. Huangfu Song wished to defy his summons, yet disregarded Liang Yan’s counsel and ultimately settled for the petty fidelity of an ordinary man. When a general is in the field, there are commands from his ruler that he does not accept: Fan Li understood this, but Huangfu Song did not.

Wu Qi personally packed and carried provisions [?], sharing his soldiers’ toil and hardship; he defended Hexi and resisted the armies of powerful Qin. Song Yi held a great drinking banquet, heedless of his soldiers’ cold and hunger; he lingered at Anyang and brought upon himself execution by Xiang Yu. One should love one’s soldiers as one loves one’s children: Wu Qi understood this, but Song Yi did not. As for these several generals and their relation to the principles of warfare, those who accorded with them succeeded, while those who contravened them failed.

text:
所謂合之者知兵法者也不合者不知兵
法者也兵法之常也高陵不可向也趙奢
先拒北山秦師爭山不得秦師大敗劉備
先據馬鞍山陸遜四面蹙之漢師大敗盖
遜以乗勝之兵蹙備已敗之兵是得夫激
水之疾可以漂石之意若秦師大敗則兩
軍相敵未有勝負者也豈可槩論乎祥疑
所當禁也田單令一卒為神以破燕者田
單智勇之將乗忿怒之軍志復宗國是得
===
夫能愚士卒耳目之意若郭京之敗則市
井無賴原不知兵者也豈可以同語乎陽
處父退舍於泜水此合令半濟而擊之之
法符堅駐軍于澗水揮兵使却亦合此法
也退不可止而大敗者盖堅軍無紀律耳
是豈知法令孰嚴之旨哉魏武日夜行三
百里遂先主于當陽正犯百里爭利則擒
之法唐太宗日夜行二百里追宋金剛于
雀鼠谷亦犯此法也遂破金剛而大捷者

translation_en:
…was simply because Jingang was already defeated and demoralized. Was this not precisely the meaning of “as swift as the wind”? Those said to conform to the methods of warfare certainly understand them; those who do not conform also understand them: this is adaptation in the methods of warfare. Viewed in this light, the constant is indeed constant, but variation too is constant. Sunzi said: “There are only five notes, yet the variations of those five notes cannot all be heard; there are only five colors, yet the variations of those five colors cannot all be seen; in warfare there are only the unorthodox and the orthodox, yet their variations cannot be exhausted.” Is not this single word, “adaptation,” the most essential thing in employing troops?

Yet there is another point to make. Arms are instruments of ill omen; to use them recklessly invites danger. Nevertheless, in the Zhou dynasty, during the reigns of Kings Cheng and Kang, the four quarters were free from trouble, and routes were open to the Nine Yi peoples. The Duke of Shao urged the king to “enlarge and strengthen the Six Armies,” and the Duke of Zhou urged him to “put your weapons and troops in order.” Were these two dukes guiding their ruler toward the display of military might? In times when all under Heaven is at peace, rulers commonly devote their attention to ceremonial forms and institutions, regarding these as means of embellishing an age of peace. As for military affairs, they often regard them as matters of no urgency: speaking of them is considered inauspicious, and attending to them is considered making needless trouble. When sudden upheaval occurs under Heaven, they are bewildered and have no means of responding. Villains and traitors can then give free rein to their Heaven-defying wickedness, and the realm consequently falls into great disorder. What a flourishing and powerful realm there was in the time of Tang Xuanzong! Yet at a single beat of An Lushan’s drum in Yuyang, the military commands crumbled, and the imperial carriage…

職奉法文章禮樂閭巷彬彬而愚生之慮
以為所因循而不振者兵與將耳此亦或
執事未發之意也敢僭言之謹對
第四問
張鎬
同考試官行人楊批說諸賢異同處明白
切當盖知求同於理而不泥其跡者是可與事
君矣取之非特以其文也
===

必異惟其是而已此作得之
考試官右庶子韓批人臣事君不必其跡之
同惟心之自靖耳此作能言之宜錄
君子之事君也其分則殊而其理則一焉
夫人所賦之才所處之地不能皆同則其
分不得不殊矣然不失其本然之性不違
其當然之則是則所謂理也君子惟求其
理之一耳而何必計其分之殊哉嘗觀宋

…the worthies of the Song, and thereby came to understand this principle. Cao Bin and Xiang Minzhong both deliberated on attacking the Khitan. Bin requested powerful crossbows and infantry, seeking simply to punish and execute the enemy; Minzhong, however, said that provisions were scarce, the route long, and the timing unsuitable for sending out troops: other strategies should instead be devised to bring them under control. Since an imperial army seeks victory with its strength intact, Minzhong’s strategy was superior. How could the ruler of that time fail to commend and adopt it? Even so, warfare must not be forgotten.

Bao Zheng and Ouyang Xiu both served as Prefect of Kaifeng. Zheng governed his subordinates with stern authority, ensuring that private influence could gain no access. Xiu, however, held that forcing someone to do what lay beyond his abilities would inevitably lead to failure; one should instead bring peace through simple administration that followed sound principles. Since governing the people rests upon leniency, Xiu’s chosen approach was good. How could the people of that time fail to praise its convenience and remember him fondly? Even so, severity cannot be dispensed with.

Wen Yanbo, a senior minister who had served three reigns, was exceedingly deferential in serving his sovereign. Cheng Zhengshu, summoned from private life into service, was exceedingly dignified when appearing before the sovereign. Thus arose talk of respectfulness and arrogance. People entirely failed to understand that a chief councilor serving a young ruler dared not be other than respectful in his ceremonial conduct, while a great Confucian scholar, possessing the dignity of a teacher, must uphold the weight of his Way. One was a teacher, the other a minister: Zengzi and Zisi would each have acted likewise had they exchanged positions. Was it not shallow to question Zhengshu on this account?

text:
知世臣休戚相同不得不歸以見上諍臣
風節自勵不得不退以自守出也處也禹
稷顏子易地則皆然也以是而貶申公不
亦謬乎由前四臣而言則所賦之才有不
同然皆足以定國而安民由後四臣而言
則所處之地有不同然皆足以尊君而正
己其於本然之性當然之則既皆不背而
一時人才之盛又何以加於此哉抑聞之
有大臣之度有大臣之節含弘廣大之中
===
而不可無確然之介剛毅明察之下而不
可無渾然之體固未嘗以苟同而亦未嘗
以求異也若小人則不然迹合而心離面
譽而背毀植私黨以排善類執己見以廢
大公而敗天下之事亦多矣然則人君於
君子小人之間可不深辨而密察之也哉
謹對
第五問
徐九皐

知世臣休戚相同，不得不歸以見上；諍臣風節自勵，不得不退以自守。出也，處也，禹、稷、顏子易地則皆然也。以是而貶申公，不亦謬乎？由前四臣而言，則所賦之才有不同，然皆足以定國而安民；由後四臣而言，則所處之地有不同，然皆足以尊君而正己。其於本然之性、當然之則，既皆不背，而一時人才之盛，又何以加於此哉？抑聞之，有大臣之度，有大臣之節。含弘廣大之中，而不可無確然之介；剛毅明察之下，而不可無渾然之體。固未嘗以苟同，而亦未嘗以求異也。若小人則不然，迹合而心離，面譽而背毀，植私黨以排善類，執己見以廢大公，而敗天下之事亦多矣。然則人君於君子小人之間，可不深辨而密察之也哉？謹對。

第五問

徐九皐
translation_en:
…understand that a minister from a family long in dynastic service shares the dynasty’s fortunes and must return to seek an audience with the sovereign, while a remonstrating minister holds himself to high standards of integrity and must withdraw to preserve his principles. Whether taking office or remaining in retirement, Yu, Ji, and Master Yan would each have acted likewise had they exchanged places. Is it not mistaken to disparage the Duke of Shen on these grounds? As for the first four ministers, their endowed talents differed, yet all were capable of securing the state and bringing peace to the people. As for the latter four ministers, their circumstances differed, yet all were capable of honoring their ruler and keeping their own conduct upright. Since none departed from their original nature or the principles they ought to follow, how could any age surpass this flourishing abundance of talent?

I have also heard that there is the magnanimity of a great minister, and there is the integrity of a great minister. Within capacious generosity there must be firm principle; beneath resolute strength and discerning judgment there must be an underlying wholeness. Such men neither agree merely for agreement’s sake nor seek difference for its own sake. Petty men, however, are otherwise: outwardly united, they are inwardly divided; they praise to a man’s face and disparage him behind his back. They establish private factions to exclude good men and cling to their own views at the expense of the common good. Many indeed are the affairs of the realm that they have ruined. Can a ruler, then, fail to distinguish carefully between noble and petty men and scrutinize them closely? Respectfully submitted in reply.

Fifth Question

Xu Jiugao

title: 嘉靖七年順天府鄉試錄
text:
同考試官主事吳批時政一策正欲觀士
子用世之學答者非泛則畧殊無足取此卷深
究弊源而責效於得人末復以古昔盛治為
聖天子望忠愛溢于言表豈獨取其識時務也邪
考試官右庶子方批經生乃能正論如此豈所
謂文武兼資者邪錄之以俟
考試官右庶子韓批致弊之由革弊之道是
如此
有致弊之源有拯弊之道然欲拯其弊當
===
先究其源拯弊而不究其源是猶醫者之
治病苟不究其病源之所在抑何以施治
療之法哉生也恭承明問而有以知前日
致弊之源今日拯弊之道矣天下之道二
義與利之間也天下尚義則治尚利則亂
前日之致弊者利也今日拯弊之道亦有
義而已矣仰惟
聖天子在上日勤
聖學總攬乾綱備二帝三王之德則固宜有太

title: 嘉靖七年順天府鄉試錄
text:
和雍熈之治也而天下之弊如執事所言
種種者何哉在邊陲帥臣格之也在郡縣
有司格之也自正德十六年間權奸相繼
用事政以賄成我
祖宗以来生養安全之道禮義廉恥之教綱紀
法度之制掃蕩無幾外而邊陲之将内而
郡縣之吏陟者以利而超遷黜者以利而
幸免而将與吏多不得其人矣将既不得
其人則邊陲之上軍士不得不怯怠帑藏
===
不得不空虚紀綱不得不陵遲也吏既不
得其人則郡縣之内生民不得不困瘁盜
賊不得不竊發風俗不得不頹敗也是前
日所以致是弊者無他利而已矣知前日
所以致弊之源則今日所以拯弊之道可
得而言矣盖嘗聞之士有百善惟廉為最
士有百惡惟貪為最盖廉則眾欲皆伏而
達之於政自無不善貪則眾欲皆起而達
之於政自不能善廉者義之大也貪者不

幸免而將與吏多不得其人矣將既不得
其人則邊陲之上軍士不得不怯怠帑藏
===
不得不空虛紀綱不得不陵遲也吏既不
得其人則郡縣之內生民不得不困瘁盜
賊不得不竊發風俗不得不頹敗也是前
日所以致是弊者無他利而已矣知前日
所以致弊之源則今日所以捄弊之道可
得而言矣蓋嘗聞之士有百善惟廉為最
士有百惡惟貪為最蓋廉則衆欲皆伏而
達之於政自無不善貪則衆欲皆起而達
之於政自不能善廉者義之大也貪者不
punctuated:
和雍熈之治也。而天下之弊，如執事所言種種者，何哉？在邊陲，帥臣格之也；在郡縣，有司格之也。自正德十六年間，權奸相繼用事，政以賄成。我祖宗以来，生養安全之道，禮義廉恥之教，綱紀法度之制，掃蕩無幾。外而邊陲之将，内而郡縣之吏，陟者以利而超遷，黜者以利而幸免，而将與吏多不得其人矣。将既不得其人，則邊陲之上，軍士不得不怯怠，帑藏不得不空虚，紀綱不得不陵遲也。吏既不得其人，則郡縣之内，生民不得不困瘁，盜賊不得不竊發，風俗不得不頹敗也。是前日所以致是弊者，無他，利而已矣。
知前日所以致弊之源，則今日所以拯弊之道，可得而言矣。盖嘗聞之：士有百善，惟廉為最；士有百惡，惟貪為最。盖廉則眾欲皆伏，而達之於政，自無不善；貪則眾欲皆起，而達之於政，自不能善。廉者，義之大也；貪者，不
translation_en:
…a reign of concord and flourishing harmony. Yet why does the realm suffer from the various abuses you have described? On the frontiers, military commanders obstruct its realization; in the prefectures and counties, the responsible officials obstruct it. During the sixteen years of the Zhengde reign, powerful, treacherous ministers successively controlled affairs, and government business was settled through bribes. The ways of nurturing and safeguarding the people, the teachings of ritual propriety, righteousness, integrity, and shame, and the institutions of discipline, law, and regulation established since the time of our imperial ancestors were swept away, leaving scarcely anything. Among frontier commanders outside and prefectural and county officials within, those promoted secured advancement beyond the normal grades through payments, while those facing dismissal bought undeserved exemption. Thus commanders and civil officials were often unsuitable for their posts. With unsuitable men as commanders, frontier soldiers inevitably became timid and indolent, treasuries inevitably became empty, and discipline inevitably deteriorated. With unsuitable men as civil officials, the people in the prefectures and counties inevitably suffered hardship and exhaustion, bandits inevitably rose up, and customs inevitably decayed. What brought about these abuses in the past was nothing other than the pursuit of profit.
Once we understand the source of past abuses, we can explain how to remedy them today. I have heard it said: among the hundred virtues of a scholar, integrity is foremost; among his hundred vices, greed is foremost. With integrity, all desires are subdued, and when this is carried into government, nothing fails to be good. With greed, all desires arise, and when this is carried into government, it cannot be good. Integrity is the highest expression of righteousness; greed is the highest expression of unrighteousness …

title: 嘉靖七年順天府鄉試錄
text:
義之大也是故今日之所急者義而已矣
必也絶請托之私重苞苴之禁公銓選之
法明黜陟之典則前日之私既足以驅天
下於利而今日之公獨不足以驅天下於
義乎誠使邊陲之將郡縣之吏皆忘一身
之私秉為國之公則前日之弊將不革而
自除焉不然則操演雖勤徒足以為觀聽
之具轉輸雖多徒足以長侵漁之奸誅戮
雖嚴徒足以激凶頑之怒矣邊陲何自而
===
理哉蠲賑雖頻徒足以資里書之欺捕詰
雖急徒足以貽地方之擾教戒雖切徒足
以為文具之虛矣郡縣何自而治哉遐想
古人李抱真之帥澤潞也教習步兵而天
下推勇郭子儀之至朔方也按誅亂將而
諸鎮奉法趙充國屯要害浚溝渠而興屯
田於是羌夷降敗是皆名將也得是人而
布之邊陲之上如李抱真焉何患乎軍士
之不振如郭子儀焉何患乎紀綱之不伸

punctuated:
義之大也。是故今日之所急者，義而已矣。必也絶請托之私，重苞苴之禁，公銓選之法，明黜陟之典，則前日之私既足以驅天下於利，而今日之公獨不足以驅天下於義乎？誠使邊陲之將、郡縣之吏皆忘一身之私，秉為國之公，則前日之弊將不革而自除焉。不然，則操演雖勤，徒足以為觀聽之具；轉輸雖多，徒足以長侵漁之奸；誅戮雖嚴，徒足以激凶頑之怒矣。邊陲何自而理哉？蠲賑雖頻，徒足以資里書之欺；捕詰雖急，徒足以貽地方之擾；教戒雖切，徒足以為文具之虛矣。郡縣何自而治哉？

遐想古人，李抱真之帥澤潞也，教習步兵而天下推勇；郭子儀之至朔方也，按誅亂將而諸鎮奉法；趙充國屯要害，浚溝渠而興屯田，於是羌夷降敗。是皆名將也。得是人而布之邊陲之上，如李抱真焉，何患乎軍士之不振？如郭子儀焉，何患乎紀綱之不伸？
translation_en:
…the greatest unrighteousness. Thus what is urgently needed today is righteousness alone. Surely, if we eliminate private influence through requests and intercession, enforce strict prohibitions on gifts and bribes, make the selection and appointment of officials impartial, and clarify the rules for demotion and promotion, then, since the partiality of former days was sufficient to drive all under Heaven toward profit, could the impartiality of today alone be insufficient to drive all under Heaven toward righteousness? If the frontier commanders and the officials of prefectures and counties truly put aside their personal interests and uphold impartial service to the state, the former abuses will disappear of themselves, without needing to be forcibly eradicated. Otherwise, however assiduously troops drill, it will merely provide a spectacle for eyes and ears; however abundant the transport of supplies, it will merely foster fraudulent exactions and embezzlement; and however harsh the executions, they will merely provoke the anger of the violent and recalcitrant. How, then, can order be established on the frontiers? However frequent tax remissions and relief distributions may be, they will merely furnish opportunities for village clerks to deceive; however urgent arrests and interrogations may be, they will merely bring disturbance to the locality; and however earnest instruction and admonition may be, they will merely become empty paperwork. How, then, can prefectures and counties be well governed?

Looking far back to men of old: when Li Baozhen commanded at Ze and Lu, he trained the infantry, and all under Heaven acclaimed their valor. When Guo Ziyi arrived in Shuofang, he investigated and executed rebellious commanders, and the various military commands observed the law. Zhao Chongguo stationed troops at strategic points, dredged ditches and canals, and established military agricultural colonies; thereupon the Qiang tribes surrendered or were defeated. These were all renowned generals. If we could obtain such men and station them along the frontiers—with men like Li Baozhen, why worry that the troops would lack vigor? With men like Guo Ziyi, why worry that discipline would not be enforced?…

title: 嘉靖七年順天府鄉試錄
text:
如趙充國焉何患乎帑藏之不足今武舉
之選世襲之胄多矣其中獨無是人歟文
翁之守蜀郡也建立學校而治崇禮義虞
詡之長朝歌也誘擒盜賊而人稱神明龔
遂勸農桑重牧養而禁奢侈於是郡有蓄
積是皆良吏也得是人而布於郡縣之中
如文翁焉何患乎風俗之不淳如虞詡焉
何患乎盜賊之不息如龔遂焉何患乎民
生之不安今科目之舉畿藩之貢多矣其
===
中獨無是人歟易曰蠱先甲三日後甲三
日夫天下之勢在外則邊陲在內則郡縣
今邊陲之上郡縣之內其弊如此可謂蠱
之極矣然則今日治蠱之責能無勞於
聖天子之心乎先甲後甲治蠱之道也程子曰
治蠱者先究其所以然則知救之之道後
慮其所將然則知備之之方善救則前弊
可革善備則後利可久今日拯弊之要無
踰於此者矣雖然竊又嘗究理亂之勢推

translation_en:
…With men like Zhao Chongguo, why worry that the treasury would be insufficient? Today there are many men selected through the military examinations and many scions of hereditary military families. Can there really be no such men among them? When Wen Weng served as Administrator of Shu Commandery, he established schools and made ritual propriety and righteousness central to his government. When Yu Xu served as Magistrate of Chaoge, he lured bandits into capture, and the people praised his almost divine discernment. Gong Sui encouraged farming and sericulture, emphasized livestock raising, and prohibited extravagance; consequently, the commandery accumulated reserves. These were all good officials. If men like these were found and stationed throughout the commanderies and counties—with men like Wen Weng, why worry that customs would fail to be wholesome? With men like Yu Xu, why worry that banditry would not cease? With men like Gong Sui, why worry that the people's livelihoods would be insecure? Today there are many men advanced through the civil examinations and recommended from the capital region and the provinces. Can there really be no such men among them?
The Book of Changes says: “Gu [Decay]: three days before the jia day, three days after the jia day.” As for the condition of the realm, externally it concerns the frontiers, and internally the commanderies and counties. Now abuses on the frontiers and within the commanderies and counties are such that decay may be said to have reached its utmost extent. Can the responsibility for remedying this decay today fail to burden the mind of the sagely Son of Heaven? Attending to what precedes and follows the jia day is the way to remedy decay. Master Cheng said: “Those who remedy decay first investigate how it came about, and thus understand the way to correct it; then they consider what will develop afterward, and thus understand how to guard against it. If they correct it well, former abuses can be eliminated; if they make preparations well, subsequent benefits can endure.” Nothing surpasses this as the essential means of remedying today's abuses. Nevertheless, I have also ventured to investigate the tendencies of order and disorder, and to trace…

title: 嘉靖七年順天府鄉試錄
text:
盛衰之迹乃既為今日憂而又為今日喜
書曰天閟毖我成功所然則今日
聖天子承先朝之大弊雖不能不廑宵旰之憂
而其所以弘中興之業永萬世之譽者亦
豈不在於是乎是故商道不衰無以成高
宗之名周道不衰無以見宣王之績今天
下行將太平矣明明天子令聞不已敢為
今日誦謹對

今日誦謹對
punctuated: 盛衰之迹，乃既為今日憂，而又為今日喜。《書》曰：「天閟毖我成功所。」然則今日聖天子承先朝之大弊，雖不能不廑宵旰之憂，而其所以弘中興之業、永萬世之譽者，亦豈不在於是乎？是故商道不衰，無以成高宗之名；周道不衰，無以見宣王之績。今天下行將太平矣。「明明天子，令聞不已」，敢為今日誦。謹對。
translation_en: …the traces of flourishing and decline, I find cause both to worry about the present and to rejoice in it. The Book of Documents says: “Heaven carefully safeguards our accomplishments[?].” Thus, although our sagely Son of Heaven has inherited grave abuses from the preceding reign and cannot but be troubled by cares that keep him awake at night and delay his meals until late in the day, is this not also precisely the opportunity through which he may enlarge the work of dynastic restoration and perpetuate his renown for ten thousand generations? Had the way of Shang not declined, there would have been no means of establishing Gaozong’s fame; had the way of Zhou not declined, there would have been no means of displaying King Xuan’s achievements. Now all under Heaven will soon enjoy great peace. “Illustrious is the Son of Heaven; his fair fame never ceases.” I venture to recite these words for the present day. Respectfully submitted in reply.

title: 嘉靖七年順天府鄉試錄
text:
順天府鄉試錄後序
嘉靖戊子秋八月臣邦奇臣鵬
祗奉
明詔主順天府試事取士既得錄亦
告成臣鵬序其後曰夫錄何為
者也錄其名氏也錄其文也夫
錄其名氏以為天下榮也臣獨
憂之或素無聞焉則人將驗而
訾之矣錄其文以為天下式也
臣復憂之或間有疵焉則人將
指而議之矣然文者末也而有
行焉諸士修之於家嘗思所以
自厲乎宅心必端也撿身必敬
也修辭必誠也此之謂立其體

憂之或素無聞焉則人將駭而
訾之矣錄其文以為天下式也
〔臣〕復憂之或間有疵焉則人將
指而議之矣然文者末也而有
行焉諸士修之於家嘗思所以
自厲乎宅心必端也檢身必敬
也修辭必誠也此之謂立其體
punctuated:
順天府鄉試錄後序

嘉靖戊子秋八月，臣邦奇、臣鵬祗奉明詔，主順天府試事。取士既得，錄亦告成。臣鵬序其後曰：「夫錄何為者也？錄其名氏也，錄其文也。夫錄其名氏，以為天下榮也，臣獨憂之：或素無聞焉，則人將驗而訾之矣。錄其文，以為天下式也，臣復憂之：或間有疵焉，則人將指而議之矣。然文者末也，而有行焉。諸士修之於家，嘗思所以自厲乎？宅心必端也，撿身必敬也，修辭必誠也，此之謂立其體。
translation_en:
Postface to the Record of the Shuntian Prefecture Provincial Examination

In the eighth month of autumn in the wuzi year of Jiajing (1528), your servants Bangqi and Peng reverently received the imperial edict to preside over the examination at Shuntian Prefecture. The candidates having been selected, the record too was completed. Your servant Peng appended this postface:

“What is this record for? It records their names; it records their writings. Recording their names is intended to confer honor before all under Heaven, yet I alone feel concern: if any have previously had no reputation, people will scrutinize and criticize them. Recording their writings is intended to provide models for all under Heaven, yet again I feel concern: if flaws occur here and there, people will point them out and censure them. Yet writing is secondary; there is also moral conduct. You scholars cultivate this at home: have you considered how to spur yourselves onward? Your intentions must be upright, your personal conduct disciplined and reverent, and your words sincere. This is what is meant by establishing the foundation of your character. …

title: 嘉靖七年順天府鄉試錄
text:
然行者本也而有政焉諸士舉
之於鄉將效用於世亦思所以
自奮乎立朝必正直也蒞民必
廉平也應事必勤慎也此之謂
適其用其斯以為士乎抑又有
大焉君子立德為上立功立言
次之夫立言者文之至也立功
===
政之積也立德行之成也初非
二物也諸士密邇
輦轂凡我
皇上躬行之實道化之盛巍乎之功
業煥乎之文章皆目覩而身被
之其進於是無難者他日果得
若人焉出乎其間以輔成我

punctuated: 然行者本也，而有政焉。諸士舉之於鄉，將效用於世，亦思所以自奮乎？立朝必正直也，蒞民必廉平也，應事必勤慎也，此之謂適其用。其斯以為士乎？抑又有大焉。君子立德為上，立功、立言次之。夫立言者，文之至也；立功，政之積也；立德，行之成也，初非二物也。諸士密邇輦轂，凡我皇上躬行之實、道化之盛、巍乎之功業、煥乎之文章，皆目覩而身被之。其進於是無難者。他日果得若人焉，出乎其間，以輔成我…
translation_en: Yet conduct is the foundation, and there is also governance. You gentlemen, selected in your localities and about to render service in the world, have you also considered how to spur yourselves onward? At court you must be upright; in governing the people you must be incorruptible and impartial; in handling affairs you must be diligent and circumspect. This is what it means to put your capacities to their proper use. Is this, then, sufficient to make you scholars? There is something greater still. For the gentleman, establishing virtue comes first; establishing achievements and establishing lasting words come next. Establishing lasting words is the highest attainment of literary composition; establishing achievements is the cumulative result of governance; establishing virtue is the perfection of conduct. These have never been separate things. You gentlemen live close to the imperial capital. The substance of all that our Emperor personally practices, the flourishing of his moral influence, his towering achievements, and his resplendent cultural accomplishments—all these you witness with your own eyes and experience in your own persons. title: 嘉靖七年順天府鄉試錄
text:
皇明億萬年無疆之治則主司豈惟
無憂固樂之矣何樂乎盖得英
才以為天下用也
右春坊右庶子兼翰林院修撰
方鵬謹序

punctuated:
皇明億萬年無疆之治，則主司豈惟無憂，固樂之矣。何樂乎？盖得英才以為天下用也。
右春坊右庶子兼翰林院修撰方鵬謹序。
translation_en:
…our august Ming dynasty’s boundless good governance for countless millions of years, then how could the presiding examiners merely be free of concern? They would indeed rejoice in it. In what would they rejoice? In having obtained outstanding talents for service to all under Heaven.
Preface respectfully composed by Fang Peng, Right Junior Supervisor of Instruction in the Right Secretariat of the Heir Apparent and concurrently Senior Compiler in the Hanlin Academy.
